en: 1. The Section on Impermanence:
Having dispelled the sloth and torpor that have arisen, and having gladdened the mind here, [one should abandon] sloth and torpor.
Listen, for I shall proclaim this inspired utterance (udāna) spoken by the Jina.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, the all-knowing protector,
the compassionate seer who bears his final body.
Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
for having arisen, they cease, and their subsiding is bliss.
What joy, what pleasure can there be when things are thus ablaze? You have entered into darkness; why do you not seek a lamp?
Having seen these bones, cast away and scattered in every direction, pigeon-colored— what delight can there be in this?
On whatever first night a human dwells in the womb, he departs from there unestablished; once gone, he does not return.
Some great crowds seen in the evening are not seen in the morning;
and some great crowds seen in the morning are not seen in the evening.
In this regard, what mortal would place his trust in life, thinking "I am young"?
For men and women, even when young, die many times over.
Some perish in the womb, while others perish in the birth-chamber.
For some have crawled about, while others have run around.
Those who are old, those who are young, and those who are middle-aged—
men go forth into homelessness one after another, like ripe fruit from its bond.
Just as ripe fruits are always in fear of falling,
so too is a mortal who has been born always in fear of death.
Just as a vessel made of clay by a potter must all end in breaking, so too is the life of a mortal.
Just as whatever is sown in a spread-out field becomes little that remains to be harvested, so too is the life of a mortal.
Just as [the clay] is fashioned into a jar, so too is the life of a mortal.
Just as a mountain river flows onward and does not turn back,
so too the life of human beings passes away and does not return.
Whether small or great, that which is joined with suffering perishes very quickly, like a line drawn with a stick upon water.
Just as a cowherd drives his cattle to the pasture with a staff,
even so do disease, old age, and death drive the life-span of human beings.
For days and nights pass away and life is cut short;
the lifespan of mortals wanes like water in small streams.
...and life itself is cut short.
Long is the night for one who stays awake; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for the fool who does not understand the true Dharma.
"I have a son, I have wealth"—thus the fool is distressed.
For the self itself does not belong to the self; whose son is there, and whence is there wealth?
At the time of death...
many thousands and hundreds of men and women,
having indeed gathered all their enjoyments, fall under the power of death.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
All sentient beings shall die, for life indeed ends in death; according to their karma, beings will go forth, reaping the fruits of merit and evil.
Those of evil deeds go to hell, while those who have performed meritorious acts go to a good rebirth;
others, however, having cultivated the path here, shall attain nirvana, free from outflows.
Neither in the intermediate space, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft among the mountains can one find such a place.
There is no spot on earth where death could not overcome one who stands there.
Those beings who have been here, or those who will be here again—all shall depart, leaving the body behind.
Knowing this universal loss, the wise person, established in the Dharma, should lead the holy life.

Having seen here one who was decrepit, and likewise one who was diseased, and having seen one who was dead with his senses departed, that steadfast man abandoned the bonds of home; for the desires of the world are not easily cast off.
O King, indeed, even most splendid chariots wear out, and likewise the body also undergoes decay;
but the dharma of the virtuous does not undergo decay, for the virtuous communicate it to other virtuous ones.
Fie on you, O vulgar old age; for you are indeed the maker of deformity, since the body, so pleasing to the mind, has been crushed by you.
Even he who lives for a hundred years is destined for death;
for old age, or disease, or the Ender (Antaka) assails him.
For they always go forth never to return, being dissolved day and night;
like fish indeed, they are intensely tormented by the suffering of birth and death to which they are joined.
Life, whether one is moving or standing still, by day or by night, passes away like the current of rivers; it goes on and does not return.
For those whose lifespan becomes ever more diminished as night and day pass away—
like fish in shallow water, what joy can there be for them?
This form is utterly decayed, a nest of disease, and fragile;
it will undoubtedly break apart as putrid matter, for life indeed ends in death.
Alas, before long this body shall lie upon the earth—
empty, devoid of consciousness, like discarded husks.
What is the use of this body, which is ever oozing and putrid?
By one who is constantly overcome by disease and terrified of old age and death.
By means of this foul body, which is diseased and fragile,
attain supreme peace and unsurpassed security.
"I shall spend the rains here, as well as the winter and the summer"—
thus the fool thinks, failing to see the obstacle.
O son, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village, so does Death carry off that man who is intoxicated by his children and whose mind is distracted;
sons are not for protection, nor are father or kinsmen.
For those who are overcome by the Ender, there are indeed no protectors.
"This has been done by me; this remains to be done; having done this, it will be accomplished"—while mortals are thus trembling with such thoughts, old age and death crush them.
Therefore, always delighting in meditation, composed, ardent, and seeing the end of birth and old age,
may you, O monks, having overcome Māra together with his army, reach the further shore of birth and death.
2. Chapter on Desire:
O Desire, I know your root; you are born from conceptualization (saṃkalpa). I shall no longer conceptualize you; therefore, you shall not exist for me.
From desires arises sorrow; from desires arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from desires, there is no sorrow—how could there be fear?
From pleasures arises sorrow; from pleasures arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from pleasures, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?
Sweet at first but bitter in their ripening, these desires— though they seem delightful— are indeed like a firebrand that burns the foolish when it is not released from the hand.
The Noble Ones say that the bond made of iron, wood, or *balbaja* grass is not a firm bond;
rather, it is the attachment of one with a passionate mind and dull intellect who gazes longingly upon children and wife.
The Noble Ones say that this is a firm bond, secure on all sides and difficult to release;
yet, having severed even this, they go forth as wanderers, indifferent, having abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires.
Those various beautiful things in the world are not themselves desires; rather, a person’s desire is the passion of their conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa-rāga*).
Those beautiful things remain just as they are in the world; yet here, the wise subdue their longing (*chanda*).
Among human beings, there are no eternal desires; rather, desires are impermanent, and it is therein that those who long for them are bound.
Having abandoned those [fetters], however, for the sake of non-rebirth, I declare that death is no longer to be found.
For one who has generated desire, yet lets it flow away and remains undisturbed in mind,
with a heart unattached to sensual pleasures, is called "one whose stream flows upward."
Step by step, little by little, moment by moment, the wise person should blow away their own impurities, just as a smith refines silver.
Just as a chariot-maker cuts leather to fashion a sandal,
whatever desires one abandons, each of those becomes happiness.
If one desires all happiness, one should renounce all sensual pleasures;
for by renouncing all sensual pleasures, one prospers in ultimate happiness.
As long as one pursues desires, one does not attain satisfaction of the mind;
therefore, those who perceive renunciation are truly satisfied, for they are well-satisfied through wisdom.
Satisfaction through wisdom is superior; for one is not satiated by desires.
Thirst does not bring a man who is satisfied by wisdom under its control.
For men are greedy for sensual pleasures and, being heedless, alas, they delight in what is unrighteous;
they do not perceive the obstacle while their life is still so brief.
Enjoyment destroys the one of dull wit, but it does not destroy here the seeker of the self.
The dull-witted person, through cravings for enjoyments, destroys both himself and others.
For no satisfaction is found through desires, even with a rain of gold coins;
having realized that desires offer only a meager taste of pleasure, the wise man [turns away from them].
Even toward divine pleasures, he finds no delight;
the disciple of the Buddhas always delights in the destruction of craving.

Even a mountain of gold equal to the Himavat would not be enough for one person; knowing this, one should live with equanimity. For how could a person who knows suffering and its cause take delight in sensual desires?
For having recognized that the substratum in the world is indeed a thorn, the wise person should train for its very removal.
3. The Chapter on Craving:
For a person tormented by discursive thoughts, possessed of intense passion, and perceiving beauty, craving increases further; indeed, he makes this bond exceedingly tight.
But he who delights in the subsiding of discursive thought (*vitarka*), who always meditates on the foul with mindfulness—
truly, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) will be abandoned by him, and he indeed causes his bondage to rot.
These people, cast into the net blinded by desire, are shrouded by craving.
The heedless, bound in bondage like fish in the mouth of a net,
come to old age and death just as a calf seeks its mother who is full of milk.
For a person who wanders heedlessly, craving grows like a *mālatī* creeper;
indeed, he transmigrates again and again, like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit.
Indeed, beings possess streams of affection and feelings of endearment;
those men who are bound by pleasure and seek after happiness are subject to birth and old age.
Enveloped by cravings, living beings run about like hares in a snare;
clinging through fetters to attachment, they undergo suffering again and again for a long night.
Bound by craving, beings with minds stained by passion dwell in existence after existence;
those people are joined to Māra through such attachment, for they lack security and peace.
Indeed, because these attachments are difficult to transcend, they come to old age and death.
But the monk who, having abandoned craving here, is free from craving toward existence and non-existence,
who is devoid of craving and desireless, has attained final nirvana.
For him who endures this worldly craving so difficult to abandon,
sorrows increase like *bīraṇa* grass drenched by rain.
But for one who abandons this worldly craving so difficult to abandon,
his sorrows cease, like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
Therefore, I speak this auspicious word to all of you who have gathered here:
dig up craving by its very root, just as one seeking fragrant *uśīra* root digs up the *bīraṇa* grass.
When craving has been dug out by the roots, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?

Thirst is the companion of man; through longing, he wanders again and again over the long journey, entering the womb again and again. Thus, through becoming and other-becoming, he undergoes coming and going within saṃsāra.
Having abandoned that craving here, become free from craving regarding existence;
he will not wander in saṃsāra again, for craving no longer exists within him.
"By which gods and humans, seeking their welfare, remain bound; cross over this attachment! Let not the moment pass you by, for those who have let the moment pass grieve when cast into the hells."
For craving is the cause, a clinging torrent that is ever-spreading here like a net;
by completely removing this creeper of thirst, this suffering that recurs again and again comes to an end.
Just as a tree, even when cut down, grows forth once again if its roots are not harmed,
so too, as long as the latent tendencies of craving have not been uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.
Just as a firmly fixed arrow, once discharged with force by one's own hand, may strike down that very person who aimed it,
so too do the creepers of craving arising from within oneself lead to the destruction of living beings in this world.
Having understood this danger— that craving is the source of suffering—
a monk who is free from craving, without grasping, and mindful, should wander forth.
4. The Chapter on Heedfulness:
Heedfulness is indeed the state of immortality; heedlessness is the state of death.
Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if dead already.
Having understood this distinction of heedfulness,
the wise and noble person should always take delight in heedfulness, which is their own proper domain.
Those who are heedful, constant, and always firm in their exertion—
the wise ones— touch Nirvana, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
When the wise man dispels heedlessness with heedfulness,

having ascended the clarity of wisdom, he remains sorrowless while gazing upon the grieving people; like one standing on a mountain peak, the steadfast one looks down upon those who are like children on the ground.
By means of upright conduct, heedfulness, self-restraint, and self-control, the wise person makes an island; the flood does not overwhelm it.
For one who is industrious, mindful of the self, pure in heart, observant in conduct, restrained,
living according to the Dharma, and vigilant, fame increases.
Do not be negligent regarding the higher mind; train constantly in the steps of silence.
For one who is protected, who is tranquil, and whose self is always mindful, sorrows do not come to pass.
One should not cultivate base qualities, nor dwell in negligence;
one should not take pleasure in false views, nor become a prosperer of the world.
Whoever possesses even a superior degree of mundane right view does not go to a miserable rebirth, even for thousands of lifetimes.
Foolish people of dull intellect follow after negligence,
but the wise man guards heedfulness as a merchant guards his most precious wealth.
Foolish people of dull intellect follow after negligence;
however, one who is always heedful and meditative attains the destruction of the outflows.
One should not indulge in negligence, nor in the company of those who delight in sensual pleasures;
for one who is ever vigilant and meditative attains indeed the unshakable bliss.
This is not the time for negligence, for the destruction of the outflows has not yet been attained;
Māra follows one who is negligent, just as a lioness follows a lion.
A man who is heedless and who consorts with another's wife falls into four states:
the acquisition of demerit, an unwanted bed, reproach as the third, and hell as the fourth.
Seeing the acquisition of demerit and a wretched rebirth, as well as the meager pleasure of one who is afraid with those who are afraid,
and observing both the censure [of society] and the punishment from the king, one should avoid the wives of others.

There is the acquisition of demerit and a miserable rebirth; for one who is afraid, there is but meager pleasure with those who are afraid. Furthermore, the king inflicts heavy punishment, and after the dissolution of the body, he is seen in the hells.
A wise person should act with foresight regarding whatever they know to be for their own benefit; they should not exert themselves sluggishly with the deliberations of a mere cart-driver.
Just as a cartwright, having abandoned a level highway and a great road,
enters upon a rugged path and grieves bitterly when his axle breaks.
Thus, having departed from Dharma and followed Adharma,
the fool falls under the power of death and grieves like one whose eyes have been plucked out.
That which ought to be done is neglected, while that which ought not to be done is performed again;
for those who are arrogant and heedless, their taints increase.
Their taints continue to grow, and they remain far from the destruction of the taints.
But for those whose mindfulness directed toward the body is always well-undertaken,
they do not perform what should not be done; being constant in their performance of what is to be done,
the taints of those who are mindful and clearly comprehending come to an end.
One is not a bearer of the Dharma merely by speaking much;
rather, he who, having heard even a little of the Dharma here, touches it with his very body—
he indeed is a bearer of the Dharma, who does not neglect the Dharma.
Even if he speaks much that is well-composed here, a man who is negligent does not become a doer of it;
like a cowherd merely counting the cows of others, he does not partake in the goal of the ascetic life.
But even if he speaks only a little that is well-composed, he indeed becomes one who lives in accordance with the Dharma.
Having abandoned passion, hatred, and likewise delusion, one becomes a partaker of the goal of asceticism.
They praise heedfulness; heedlessness is always censured.
Through heedfulness, Maghavat attained preeminence among the gods.
The wise always praise heedfulness in one's duties;
for the wise person who is heedful secures both goals.
There is one benefit pertaining to the present life, and likewise another pertaining to future lives;
for it is through the realization of these benefits that a steadfast person is called wise.

The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness pulls himself out from the abyss, like an elephant stuck in the mud. The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness pulls himself out from the abyss, like an elephant stuck in the mud.
He shakes off evil states, just as the wind blows away leaves.
The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness goes forth like a fire, burning away fetters both subtle and gross.
The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness will,
by following the gradual path, touch the destruction of all fetters.
The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness penetrates the peaceful state,
the blissful cessation of conditioned formations.
The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness is incapable of falling away;
he is indeed close to Nirvana.
Arise, exert yourselves, and train firmly for the sake of peace!
For lack of mindfulness, negligence, lack of effort, and lack of self-restraint—these are the obstacles.
Sleep, drowsiness, and lack of application—these are obstacles to the training. Understand these factors well, lest mindfulness be lost within you.
One should rise up, not be negligent, and practice the well-performed Dharma.
For one who practices the Dharma sleeps happily both in this world and in the next. O monks, be devoted to heedfulness; be of virtuous conduct.
With well-composed intentions, protect your own minds.
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut.
For whoever shall be heedful in this Dharma and Discipline—
Having abandoned the cycle of birth, he will go to the end of suffering.
5. On the Chapter of the Dear:
From the dear arises sorrow; from the dear arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from the dear, there is no sorrow—how could there be fear?
From beloved things arises sorrow; from beloved things arises fear;
through the alteration of beloved things, one even goes to madness.

For indeed, whatever sorrows, lamentations, and manifold sufferings exist in the world, all of them arise here in dependence upon what is dear; if that which is dear did not exist, none of this would ever come to be.

Therefore, those for whom there is no object of affection whatsoever are indeed happy and free from sorrow. Thus, one who seeks the state beyond sorrow should not form attachments in this world of living beings.
May there never be union with those who are dear, nor may there ever be [union] with those who are not dear;
for the sight of the beloved is suffering, as is the sight of the unbeloved.
From the loss of loved ones and from the encounter with those who are disliked,
intense sorrow arises by which human beings are worn away.
When a loved one has died and passed away, kinsmen stand together and grieve for the long road ahead; for union with what is dear is indeed sorrowful.
Therefore, one should not cultivate affection, for the state of affection is evil. Those for whom there is neither the liked nor the disliked have no knots [of attachment].
Always yoking the self during the non-yoke and unyoking it during the yoke.
Having abandoned the meaning, one who clings to the literal expression longs for a person endowed with wealth.
The bodies of gods, though bound by the seven attachments to pleasant forms and existing separately,
are afflicted with grief, utterly exhausted, and have fallen under the power of the King of Death.
Those who, both by day and by night, being ever vigilant, abandon what is dear—
they indeed dig up the root of evil, that bait of death which is so difficult to overcome.
The unwholesome under the guise of the wholesome, the unpleasant under the guise of the pleasant,
and suffering under the guise of happiness— these crush those who are heedless.
If one should know oneself to be dear, one should not join it with evil;
for happiness is not easily obtained by one who performs wicked deeds.
If one should know oneself to be dear, one should not join oneself with evil;
for this happiness is easily obtained by one who performs good deeds.
If one should know oneself to be dear, one should protect it well-guarded,
as one would a frontier city that is firm and has deep moats;
a wise person should remain vigilant during at least one of the three watches of the night.
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should guard it well-guarded, just as a frontier city is guarded—secure both within and without. Thus should you guard yourselves; let not the moment pass you by.
For those who have passed even a single moment [of heedlessness] grieve when cast into the hells.

Having traversed all directions with his mind, he did not find anywhere anyone dearer than himself; thus, the self is equally dear to others. Therefore, one should not harm another for the sake of one's own self.
All fear punishment; life is dear to all.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause another to kill.
Just as kinsmen, friends, and companions rejoice upon the arrival of a long-traveling wayfarer who has returned safely from afar, so do they welcome him when he comes.
Likewise, when a mortal who has performed meritorious deeds passes from this world to the next,
it is his very merits that welcome him, as if a beloved kinsman had returned.
Therefore, accumulate a store of merit for the sake of the future life;
for in the world beyond, merit alone is the firm foundation of living beings.
The gods praise merit and the practice of equanimity for one who would perform it;
such a person becomes irreproachable in this world and rejoices in heaven after death.
People hold dear that person who stands firm in the Dharma, is endowed with virtue, possesses a sense of shame, speaks the truth, and acts for his own spiritual welfare.
One becomes beloved by others and acts for one's own benefit as well;
in this present life one is praised, and in the future life one attains a good rebirth.
One should instruct and admonish them, and restrain them from what is improper;
thus one does not become dear to the wicked, but becomes dear to the virtuous.
Both the non-virtuous and the virtuous go in different directions after passing away from here:
the non-virtuous go to hell, while the virtuous have heaven as their ultimate destination.
6. The Chapter on Virtue:
A wise person, desiring the three kinds of happiness—namely, praise, the acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death—should guard their virtue.
Perceiving these states, the wise person should guard their virtue;
being noble and perfected in vision, they attain peace in this world.
The undertaking of ethical discipline is happiness; the body is not tormented by fever. One sleeps happily at night and awakens joyful.
Virtue is good until old age; faith is good when firmly established;
wisdom is indeed the jewel of men, a merit difficult for thieves to steal.
Having performed meritorious deeds, being wise, having given gifts, and being virtuous,
he attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
A monk established in moral discipline, with his sense faculties well-restrained,
moderate in eating, and devoted to wakefulness;
Dwelling thus, ardent and untiring day and night,
he is incapable of falling away and is indeed close to Nirvana.
A monk established in virtue should cultivate the mind and wisdom;
ardent and discerning, he shall constantly attain the destruction of suffering.
Therefore, one should constantly be observant of moral conduct, a guardian of meditative concentration,
and should train in insight while being clearly comprehending and mindful.
But he, whose fetters are destroyed, whose pride is extinguished, and who is free from substrate—
being liberated, even with his wisdom intact, does not enter into reckoning upon the dissolution of the body.
He for whom morality, concentration, and wisdom are well-cultivated is one who has reached the ultimate goal; he is stainless, free from sorrow, and has exhausted the possibility of rebirth.
For he who is liberated from attachment, O Asita, is one who has realized the truth and is free from the substratum of existence;
having transcended the realm of Māra, he shines like the sun.
For a monk who is agitated and negligent,
his virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment.
It rains upon what is covered, but it does not rain upon what is uncovered.
Therefore, one should uncover what is covered; thus, it will not rain upon him.
Seeing this, the wise person should always train in the moral precepts.
One should quickly purify the path leading to nirvāṇa.
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor that of tagara or sandalwood produced by fire;
but the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind—the person of noble character wafts in all directions.
Compared to these varieties of fragrance— tagara, sandalwood, vārṣikā, and likewise the blue lotus— the fragrance of ethical discipline is unsurpassed.
Trifling indeed is this scent of tagara and sandalwood;
but the fragrance of those who possess virtuous conduct wafts even among the gods here. Such is the scent of those whose morality is pure and who dwell in heedfulness.
Māra finds no path to those who are liberated through perfect knowledge.
This is the path leading to security; this is the path for purification.
Those who practice meditation and have entered upon it will abandon the bonds of Māra.
7. The Chapter on Good Conduct:
One should guard against bodily malice and be well-restrained in body;
having abandoned bodily misconduct, one should practice good deeds with the body.
One should guard against the corruption of speech and remain restrained in words;
having abandoned misconduct of speech, one should practice good conduct through speech.
One should guard against mental malice and remain restrained in mind;
having abandoned mental misconduct, one should practice mental good conduct.
Having abandoned misconduct of body and misconduct of speech, and having abandoned misconduct of mind and whatever else is associated with fault, [one should practice virtue].
One should perform wholesome deeds with the body, much wholesome with speech,
and immeasurable wholesome deeds with the mind that lead to the absence of suffering.
Having performed wholesome deeds with body, speech, and mind,
one attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
The sages are indeed non-violent and always restrained in body;
they go to the imperishable state, having reached which one does not grieve.
The sages who are indeed non-violent and always well-restrained in speech go to the imperishable state, having gone to which one does not grieve.
The sages are indeed non-violent and are always restrained in mind;
they go to the imperishable state, having reached which one does not grieve.
The wise are restrained in body; the wise are well-restrained in speech;
the wise are restrained in mind; the wise are restrained in every way.
They go indeed to the imperishable state, having gone to which they do not grieve.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is good;
restraint of the mind is good; restraint in all things is good. A monk who is restrained in all things is liberated from all suffering.
Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind, and likewise not performing unwholesome acts with the body—
one who purifies these auspicious paths of action shall attain the Path proclaimed by the Seers.
8. The Chapter on Speech:
One who speaks what is untrue goes to the hells, as does one who performs other such actions here;
for both these men, having practiced inferior dharmas, are declared to be equal after death in the next world.
For a man who is born, an axe is indeed born in his mouth,
with which he cuts himself by speaking ill-spoken words.
He who praises those who deserve blame and blames those who deserve praise gathers that strife with his own mouth; by means of that strife, he finds no happiness.
Trifling indeed is this misfortune, that one might lose wealth here through dice;
far greater than this is the misfortune here, that one should harbor malice toward the Sugatas.
One hundred thousand, sixty-three million, and five hundred thousand *arbudas*—
these are the hells that one who reviles the Noble Ones enters, having directed his speech and mind toward evil.
For those of evil mind speak what is untrue; it constantly increases hell for their own destruction.
But one who possesses blameless strength endures that, having abandoned the turbidity of the mind.
For he who upholds the teaching of the Arhats, the Noble Ones who live according to the Dharma—
The one of dull wit reviles while relying on an evil view;
he should abandon what is beautiful, but never abandon what is evil. It is better to be released from what is beautiful, for when released from what is evil, one shines.
One who is already liberated should not release that [mind]; for one who releases it while still bound is afflicted.
The Noble Ones do not release it in this way; for they are liberated, whereas the wicked [state] belongs to fools.
A monk who is restrained in speech, speaking slowly and without arrogance, teaches both the meaning and the Dharma; his speech is sweet.
The Noble Ones have said that well-spoken words are supreme: first, one should speak the Dharma and not what is contrary to the Dharma;
second, one should speak what is pleasant and not what is unpleasant; third, one should speak the truth and not what is untrue; and fourth, [the same].
One should speak only that speech by which one does not torment oneself and does not harm others; for such speech is well-spoken.
One should always speak only what is pleasant, for by such speech one is welcomed;
and while speaking what is always agreeable, one does not incur any evil.
Speech should be truthful and immortal, for truthful speech is indeed unsurpassed;
they say that speech is firmly established in truth regarding both meaning and the Dharma.
That speech which the Buddha speaks— secure, leading to the attainment of Nirvana,
and joined with the end of suffering— that indeed is well-spoken speech.
9. Karma Chapter:
For a person who has transgressed even a single dharma of false speech and has passed over to the next world, there is no evil deed that they would not commit.
For it is better to eat glowing iron balls resembling tongues of fire than for one of evil character and unrestrained mind to consume the alms-food of a kingdom.
If you fear suffering, and if suffering is unpleasant to you,
do not commit an evil deed, whether openly or in secret.
If you will perform or are performing evil deeds,
there is no liberation for you from suffering, even if you were to leap up and flee.
Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor having entered a cleft among the mountains—
there is no spot on earth where one might stand and not be overcome by karma.
The black and white deeds of an embodied being do not perish;
having been performed and accumulated, they reach fruition when their time arrives.
Whatever evil deed one may see others performing here, one should not do that oneself; for by such an evil deed, one is bound.
Those who employ false measures and engage in dishonest actions—
Those people who harm human beings, whether by their own initiative or through the instigation of others,
indeed fall into a precipice, for those people are bound by their own karma.
Whatever action a person performs, whether auspicious or evil, of that very action he is the heir; for indeed, action does not perish.
For a person plunders as much as he can arrange;
then others plunder him, and that plunderer is himself plundered.
For while committing [evil], the fool thinks, "This will not come upon me";
but in the next world, he realizes what the destination is for those of sinful deeds.
For the fool, while committing [the act], thinks: "This will not come upon me";
but later, it becomes bitter for one who has indulged in its ripening.
If a fool, while performing evil deeds, does not realize it,

that person of poor intellect suffers as if burnt by fire because of his own actions. Indeed, fools of wicked wisdom behave as if they were with enemies, even though they are acting toward themselves.
Performing evil deeds, which result in bitter fruit.
That action is not well done which, having been performed, one later regrets;
for one must experience its ripening while weeping with a tearful face.
But that action is well done which, having been performed, one does not regret;
it is that whose ripening one experiences with confidence and a joyful mind.
Seeking their own pleasure, they commit evil deeds while laughing;
yet, suffering, they experience the ripening of those deeds while weeping.
For an evil deed committed does not coagulate immediately like milk.
Consuming that child, it follows him like a fire covered by ashes.
For an evil deed committed does not cut like a sword immediately;
rather, one learns of it in the hereafter, which is the destination of those who perform evil deeds.
But later, it becomes bitter for the one who indulged in it, when its ripening occurs.
For rust that has arisen from iron, once it has emerged, consumes that very iron;
in the same way, one's own actions lead one who acts without reflection to a state of misery.
10. The Chapter on Faith (Śraddhāvarga):
Faith, then modesty, virtue, and also generosity—these qualities are praised by noble persons.
For they call this the divine path; by means of it, one goes to the world of the gods.
The miserly do not indeed go to the world of the gods, for they are fools who do not praise giving;
but one who rejoices even in another's gift, through that very act, becomes happy in the next world.
For faith is the best wealth of a person; dharma well-practiced brings happiness.
Truth is indeed the sweetest of flavors; wisdom is said to be the best livelihood among those who live.

For faith is the wealth of the Arhats; one who desires to hear the Dharma for the sake of attaining Nirvana becomes wise in each and every respect. Through faith, one indeed crosses the flood, and through heedfulness, the ocean.
Through vigor one abandons suffering; through wisdom one becomes completely purified.
Faith becomes the companion of a person, and wisdom instructs him;
the monk who delights in Nirvana cuts through the bonds of existence.
He who possesses faith and virtue, as well as non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control— he, having cast off all faults and being wise, is called one of noble form.
One who is faithful, endowed with virtue, generous, and free from envy is honored wherever he may go.
Whatever wise person in this world obtains faith and wisdom—that indeed is their supreme wealth; all other wealth is inferior.
One whose desire is for the vision of the noble ones, who delights in hearing the true Dharma,
and who has removed the stain of stinginess— he indeed is called "one possessed of faith."
The faithful person takes as provisions for the journey merit, which is very difficult for thieves to steal;
he wards off the thief who would rob it, and thus the monks who take away [his wealth] become dear to him.
Seeing that the monks have arrived, the wise rejoice.
Some people give according to their faith and according to their means;
in that regard, he who becomes displeased at the food and drink of others does not attain meditative concentration by day or by night.
But he for whom these [defilements] have been completely cut off, struck down like the tops of palm trees—
he indeed attains meditative concentration by day and by night.
One should not serve one who is devoid of faith, just as one would not approach a lake that has no water; for even if one were to dig there, one might find only water smelling of mud.
One should serve a wise man who performs ancestral rites (śrāddha), just as one seeking water resorts to a lake that has clear water, is serene, possesses cool water, and is undisturbed.
One should not become attached to those who are not devoted; for in such a case, people indeed suffer a rupture.
Avoiding those who lack faith, he attends upon those who have faith.
[10. The Chapter on Faith] Impermanence, sensual desire, and craving; likewise, heedfulness is dear. Virtuous conduct, well-spoken speech, action, and faith—these are the ten.
11. Śramaṇa Chapter:
Exerting yourself, cut off the stream; drive away all sensual desires.
Without abandoning sensual desires, a sage does not attain singleness.
For a wise person acting thus should always exert firm effort;
for a lax state of renunciation surely takes up the dust of worldly passion once again.
Whatever action is slack, or whatever austerity is afflicted,
or whatever holy life is impure— that does not yield great fruit.
Just as a poorly grasped arrow cuts the very hand that holds it,
so too a wrongly practiced ascetic life drags one down into the hells.
Just as an arrow well-grasped does not cut the hand,
so the ascetic life, when properly embraced, brings one close to Nirvana.
The life of a recluse is difficult to practice and hard to endure for one of dull intellect; there are many obstacles therein where the dull-witted man desponds.
But he who practices the life of a recluse yet fails to restrain his own mind will sink again and again, having fallen under the power of his conceptual constructions.
Difficult is the going forth, difficult is the delighting therein, and difficult is the dwelling in the household life.
Painful is association with those who are not equal, and painful are the accumulated states of existence.
Indeed, many are those with saffron robes around their necks who possess evil qualities and are unrestrained.
For by their evil deeds, the wicked go from here to a miserable rebirth;
he who is utterly immoral makes himself just as an enemy would wish for him, like a *mālatī* creeper clinging to a *sāla* tree.
One does not become an elder merely by having a gray head;
his age is merely ripe, and he is called one who is worn out by delusion.
But he who, having abandoned both merit and evil, lives the holy life and wanders having detached from all worldly ties— he indeed is called a "Venerable" (sthavira).
One is not a śramaṇa merely by virtue of being shaven-headed; for one who speaks untruth and is unrestrained, being possessed by desire and greed—how can such a person be a śramaṇa?

One is not a *śramaṇa* merely by virtue of being shaven-headed; for one who speaks falsehood is not restrained. He by whom evil has been pacified in every respect—whether subtle or gross—is indeed called a *śramaṇa* because of that pacification of evils.
A brahmin is one who has cast out evils; a śramaṇa is one who has stilled what is unwholesome;
and having caused the impurities to go forth, one is called a pravrajita here in this world.
12. The Chapter on the Path:
When one perceives the four noble truths with wisdom, one understands this path that utterly destroys craving for existence.
For just as rising dust is stilled by rain,
so too are mental constructions stilled when one perceives with wisdom.
For this wisdom that leads to disenchantment is indeed the best in this world;
by means of it, one correctly understands the destruction of birth and death.
Among paths, the eightfold is supreme; among truths, the four noble ones.
Among phenomena, dispassion is supreme; and among bipeds, the one with vision is supreme.
When one perceives with wisdom that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
When one perceives with wisdom that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
When one perceives all conditioned phenomena as empty through wisdom, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
When one perceives with wisdom that all phenomena are without self, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
I have declared to you the path that cuts through the thorn of ignorance;
now it is for you yourselves to practice it, for those who have attained suchness are merely teachers.
I have taught you the path that cuts out the thorn of craving;
for the Tathāgatas are merely teachers—the work is to be done by you yourselves.
For this is the path, and no other exists, for the purification of vision;
those who have entered it and practice meditation shall abandon the bonds of Māra.
This is indeed the direct path, and this alone is the way of supreme effort, like the flight of a swan through a lake;
Śākyamuni, being fully concentrated, has realized it and proclaims it repeatedly among his assemblies.
This one who perceives the end of birth, old age, and death speaks this path out of compassion for our welfare;
for by this path, those who have crossed over, those who are crossing, and those who will cross the flood have done so.
For ultimate steadfastness, for self-control, for purity, for the exhaustion of birth and death in saṃsāra,
and for the analytical knowledge of the manifold elements— this very path has been proclaimed by the Knower of the World.
Just as the waters of the Gaṅgā, having departed from their faults, flow together with the ocean,
even so this path shown by the Sugata flows toward the attainment of the deathless.

One should always pay homage to such a being, the foremost among gods and men, who out of compassion for all living beings set in motion the Wheel of Dharma never heard before, and who has reached the further shore of existence. One should always cultivate wholesome thoughts and always avoid unwholesome ones.
Then one will abandon both applied thought and sustained thought, just as rain washes away rising dust.

Through the stilling of applied thought, he shall touch with his mind the unsurpassed bliss of awakening; having cultivated immeasurable, pure concentration born of seclusion, he should bind it fast with his mind. Having demolished the three abodes, the prudent and mindful one abandons the three bonds.
Armed with wisdom, endowed with the power of meditative concentration, composed, delighting in dhyāna, and mindful in self,
having understood the arising and passing away of the world, that knower is liberated from everything.
One who practices it properly obtains happiness if they seek happiness, and attains renown and glory from all sides—
indeed, he who cultivates the noble, direct, and auspicious Eightfold Path for the attainment of the Deathless.
13. The Chapter on Honor (Satkāravarga):
Just as the fruit destroys the plantain tree, the fruit destroys the bamboo, and the fruit destroys the reed, so does honor destroy the base man, just as the fetus destroys the mule.
For as long as a fool is known to be for one's own harm,
he destroys the virtuous portion of the fool and may even cause his head to fall off.
The unvirtuous desire gain and honor among the monks,
as well as possessiveness regarding their dwellings and veneration from the families of others.
May both householders and renunciants always know me alone;
may they be subject to my will in certain matters of what ought and ought not to be done.
Such are the intentions of the fool; desire and pride cause them to increase.
For the means to worldly gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nirvana is another.
Having understood this as it truly is, a disciple of the Buddhas should never delight in honor, but should instead increase his seclusion.
One should not strive in all things to become dependent on others;
one should not live relying on another, nor should one practice the life of a merchant for the sake of mere profit.
One should not despise what one has obtained for oneself, nor should one covet the possessions of others;
a monk who covets the possessions of others does not attain meditative concentration.
If one wishes to live happily, being intent upon the goals of the ascetic life,
one should resort to a dwelling place such as a snake’s hole or a mouse’s burrow.
If one wishes to live happily, being attentive to the goals of the ascetic life,
one should be content with whatever is obtained and cultivate a single dharma.
If one wishes to live happily, being attentive to the goals of the ascetic life,
one should not disregard the robes, drinks, or food belonging to the Saṅgha.
Even if one possesses little knowledge, if they are well-composed in their moral conduct,
the wise praise them as one of pure livelihood and free from sloth.
If that monk is a possessor of the threefold knowledge, a slayer of death, and free from outflows, [he is truly accomplished].
For those who lack true knowledge, perceiving it as "little known," treat it with contempt.
If he becomes one who possesses the threefold knowledge, a conqueror of death, and is free from outflows,
yet ignorant people, having understood him as "one of little knowledge," despise him.
If he obtains food and drink here from people,
even if he is one of evil character, he will be honored by them.
One who constantly wears the saṃghāṭī robe gains many enemies,
yet he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and seats.
Having understood this and other such disadvantages— the great danger in honors—
a monk who possesses little knowledge, is free from longing, and is mindful should wander forth as a mendicant.
This person does not live by fasting, nor is food for the sake of the heart's tranquility;
rather, food exists for the sake of maintenance. Knowing this, one should indeed practice the search for it.
For he who constantly finds in his family honor and veneration as if they were mud—such a subtle thorn is difficult to extract; such worldly respect is hard for a base man to renounce.
14. The Chapter on Malice:
For he who should become angry with one who is not angry, or commit an evil deed against one who does no wrong—suffering touches that very person, both in this world and in the next.
First he destroys himself, and afterwards he harms others;
being destroyed himself, he kills the other, just as one with a birdlime snare kills birds.
The slayer finds a slayer; the enemy encounters enemies. Likewise, the abuser finds an abuser, and the one who incurs anger finds one who incurs anger.
This is so because, apart from hearing this True Dharma, they are ignorant.
When life is thus so limited, people harbor enmity toward someone.
Separate words have arisen, and you consider them to be supreme; for while this Saṅgha is being split, you imagine these separate words to be supreme.
The kingdom of those who break bones, those who take life, those who carry off cattle, horses, and wealth,
and those who plunder the realm, becomes whole once again;
how could it not be so for you who understand this Dharma?
Those who cut through bones, those who take away life, those who seize cattle, horses, and wealth,
and those who plunder kingdoms— such is their lot when they come together.
How could it not be so for you, who understand this Dharma?
The speech of the wise that speaks within the range of sensory experience is touched by darkness;
those led astray by such deceptive speech and who strive after it are not wise.
For others do not understand that "we are striving here";
but for those who do understand this, their disputes are stilled.
"He reviled me, he struck me, he defeated me"—
for those who harbor such enmity in their hearts, that hostility is never extinguished.
"He reviled me, he spoke against me, he defeated me, he caused me to lose"—
for those who do not harbor resentment regarding these things, their enmity is stilled.
For enmities are never appeased by enmity in this world;
enmities are appeased by forbearance—this is the eternal law.
For enmity is never appeased by enmity; rather, the state of enmity is appeased by the absence of enmity.
Indeed, the pursuit of enmity is seen to lead to harm; therefore, the wise person does not engage in enmity.
If he should indeed find a prudent companion while wandering always rightly through this world,
he should wander with him, having overcome all leakages, with a contented mind and a mindful self.
Indeed, one should not find a wise companion while wandering constantly in this world;
like a king abandoning a rebellious kingdom, one should wander alone and commit no evil deeds.
While traveling, if one does not find a companion equal to oneself, one should resolutely practice solitary conduct; for there is no companionship with the foolish.
The conduct of one alone is better than having a fool as a companion;
one should wander alone and commit no evils, free from worldly desires like an elephant gone into the forest.
The conduct of one alone is better than companionship with the foolish;
one should wander alone with little concern, like an elephant in the forest.
15. The Chapter on Mindfulness: For one whose mindfulness of breathing is perfected, well-cultivated, and mastered in successive stages, just as taught by the Buddha.
He illumines this world like the moon released from the clouds.
Whether standing with body and mind thus established, or sitting, or even lying down,
the monk who remains constantly mindful, exerting himself, will attain distinction both before and after;
and having attained distinction both before and after, he shall go to the state of invisibility to the King of Death.
One who possesses constant mindfulness directed toward the body and perpetual restraint of the sense faculties,
being concentrated, shall thereby know his own nirvāṇa.
He whose mindfulness is constant and directed toward the body in every respect—
thinking "it is not, nor will it be mine; it shall not come to be, nor shall it be mine"—
and who dwells in the successive stages of meditation, shall in due time cross over attachment.
He who is wakeful, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, joyful, and serene,
investigating the teachings at the proper time— he shall transcend birth, old age, and sorrow.
Therefore, the energetic one who is mindful and vigilant should always practice wakefulness;
having abandoned the fetters of birth and old age, he brings an end to suffering right here.
Listen to me while you are awake, and awaken even when you have fallen asleep;
vigilance is better than sleep, for there is no fear for one who is vigilant.
For those devoted to wakefulness, training day and night,
and resolved upon the deathless, the taints come to an end.
Great is the gain for those people who have gone for refuge to the Buddha,
whose mindfulness directed toward the Buddha is constant by day and by night.
Blessed are those people who have gone for refuge to the Dharma,
whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Dharma both by day and by night.
Great is the gain for those people who have gone for refuge to the Saṅgha,
whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Saṅgha by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness directed toward the Buddha is constant by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Dharma by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with a perfect awakening—
those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Saṅgha by day and by night.
"O Gautama, these disciples awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the body both by day and by night."
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with perfect awakening,
for whom meditative concentrations are ever-mindful by day and by night.
O Gautama, these disciples awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness is constantly established in ethical conduct by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with perfect awakening—
those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward renunciation, both by day and by night.
O Gautama, these disciples of mine awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the gods by day and by night.
O Gautama, these disciples of mine awaken with a true awakening,
they whose minds delight in non-violence both by day and by night.
"O Gautama, these disciples of mine awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose minds delight day and night in non-malice."
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening, O Gautama,
they whose minds delight in renunciation by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening.
Those whose minds are constantly devoted to meditation, both by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama, O Gautama, awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose minds delight in solitude both by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening, O Gautama—
those whose minds delight in emptiness by day and by night. These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening in emptiness.
Those whose minds delight in the signless both by day and by night.
O Gautama, these disciples awaken with a true awakening,
they whose minds delight in the state of nothingness both by day and by night.
O Gautama, these disciples are well-awakened,
for their minds delight in meditative cultivation both by day and by night.
"O Gautama, these disciples awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose minds delight in Nirvana both by day and by night."
16. The Chapter on Miscellaneous Matters:

One should indeed attend to one's duty beforehand, lest one's duty be frustrated at the time it ought to be performed. For him who acts by attending to his duty at its proper time, his duty is never frustrated when the time for action arrives.
A person should indeed exert effort until the accomplishment of his goal;
he should perceive his own welfare in such a way that it becomes exactly as he desires it to be.
Arise, exert yourselves, and make an island for yourselves;
like a smith working silver, remove the impurity from yourselves.
For you, whose impurities have been cleansed and who are free from blemish, shall not undergo birth and old age again.
They feel shame for what is not shameful, yet they are shameless regarding what is shameful;
they see fear where there is no fear, and see no fear where there is fear.
Through the adoption of wrong views, beings go to an evil destiny.
But he who, having previously been negligent here, does not become negligent afterwards—
he illumines this world like the moon released from the clouds.
But he who, having previously been heedless here, later indeed does not become heedless— he, it is said, overcomes this attachment in the world.
Even if one goes forth as a renunciant while still young, if they apply themselves to the Buddha's teaching,
they illuminate this world like the moon released from the clouds.
Even if one goes forth as a renunciant while still young, if they apply themselves to the teaching of the Buddha, being mindful, they will completely transcend this worldly attachment.
He whose evil deed is covered over by wholesome action shines upon this world like the moon released from clouds.
He whose evil deed is covered over by wholesome action,
being mindful, transcends this attachment in the world.
He who does not burn with grief over life nor at the end of death in every respect—
he, the wise one who has seen the goal, does not grieve at the time of death.
He who does not burn at all with regard to life or at the end of death—
he, the wise one who has seen the goal, does not grieve in the midst of sorrow.
He who does not suffer at all regarding life or at the end of death—
he, the wise one who has seen the goal, truly shines in the midst of his kinsmen.
Abandoning dark qualities, cultivate the bright ones, O monks.
Having gone from home to homelessness, one should increase solitude;
and therein the noble one, having abandoned sensual desires and possessing nothing, should find delight.

For one who is always pure, the observance is always fruitful; for one who is always pure, the *poṣadha* is always fulfilled; for one whose actions are pure, the vow is always successfully accomplished.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this progeny has passion as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from passion becomes of great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; these living beings have hatred as their defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from hatred becomes of great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has delusion as its defect. Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this progeny has pride as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those who are free from pride becomes of great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this world of beings has greed as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from greed becomes of great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has craving as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those who are free from craving becomes of great fruit.
The sixth is the sovereign king: when he is impassioned, he is full of passion; when he is free from passion, he is stainless. One who is impassioned is called a fool.
For this city has bones for its ramparts and flesh and blood for its plaster;
therein are afflicted passion, hatred, pride, and hypocrisy.

For suffering always arises from a cause; not seeing this, one is indeed bound by it. But through the realization of its true nature, one abandons attachment; for outsiders cannot abandon that great flood. (17) Udakavarga.
Possessing mindfulness, they apply themselves; they do not delight in a dwelling.
Like swans abandoning a pond, they leave their home and abandon the flood.
Like swans traveling on the path of the sun, they move through the sky with the faculties of life.
The wise ones emerge from the worlds, having utterly crushed the army of Māra.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having failed to acquire wealth in their youth,
they brood in old age like aged cranes in a small pond with few fish.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having failed to acquire wealth in their youth, they lie scattered like bows, brooding over the past.
One should not think lightly of evil, saying, "It will not come to me. Even a large jar is filled by the falling of drops of water;
likewise, fools are filled with evils even by those committed little by little.
One should not think, "This merit will not come to me," for even a great jar is filled by the falling of drops of water; likewise,
the wise are indeed filled with merits, even by those performed little by little.
Those people who, having tied together a beautiful raft, constantly cross the ocean, do not truly cross the rivers;
those wise people have already crossed them.
The Blessed Buddha has crossed over and stands on dry land, O Brahmin;
the monks are bathing here, and others are binding together rafts.
What could one do with a well where water is available everywhere?
Having uprooted the very root of thirst, whom would one seek out?
Washers cleanse with water; fletchers bend the arrow with heat;
carpenters shape wood; but the wise subdue themselves.
Just as a lake that is very deep, perfectly clear, and undisturbed,
so too do the wise become serene upon hearing the true Dharma.
Like the earth, the protector is not defiled; like a pillar, he is unshakable.
For like a lake from which the mud has been removed, the wise are indeed free from impurity.
Who will conquer this earth, as well as the world of Yama together with its gods?
Who, being skillful, will select the well-taught word of Dharma like a flower?
The learner shall conquer the earth, as well as the world of Yama together with its gods;
for he, being skilled, shall select the well-taught word of Dharma like a flower.
"Cut down the forest, not the individual tree; for from the forest indeed fear arises.
Having cut down the forest together with its roots, become free from the forest, O monks."
As long as even a particle-sized fragment of the forest of attachment remains among one's kin, a person’s mind is bound to them;
indeed, he is like a calf that has been milk-fed, clinging to its mother.
Cut off indeed your own attachment, as one would a lotus from the autumnal water;
cultivate only the path of peace, the Nirvana taught by the Sugata.
Just as a beautiful flower may be colorful yet devoid of fragrance,
so too these well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not act upon them.
Just as a beautiful flower may be colorful and fragrant,
so too does well-spoken speech bear fruit for one who acts upon it.
Just as a bee departs from a flower, taking its nectar without harming its color or fragrance, so should a sage conduct himself among villages.
One should not look at the faults of others, nor at what others have done or left undone; rather, one should examine one's own conduct, whether it be consistent or inconsistent.
Just as one might fashion many garlands from heaps of flowers,
so should a mortal who has been born perform much that is wholesome.
Just as the vāgurā releases its flower during the rains, so too, O monks, should you release passion and hatred.
Just as a lotus might grow upon a heap of refuse discarded by the great road— pure-scented and delightful to the mind.
Thus, in this world which has become like a heap of refuse and is blinded by ignorance,
the disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One shine forth with wisdom.
Death carries away a person whose mind is distracted while gathering flowers, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
Death carries away a sleeping man, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
Even while gathering flowers, with his mind distracted and still unsated in desires, the Ender brings a man under his power.
While a person is busy gathering flowers with a distracted mind,
the Ender brings them under his power even before their enjoyments have arisen.
Having understood this body to be like a water-jar and having fully awakened to the nature of phenomena as a mirage,
one should cut off Māra’s flowers here and go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Having understood this body to be like foam and having fully awakened to the nature of phenomena as a mirage,
one should cut off the flowers of Māra here and go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Having understood this world to be like a water-jar and having fully awakened to the nature of phenomena as being like a mirage,
one should cut off the flowers of Māra here and go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Having understood this world to be like foam and having fully realized that all phenomena are like a mirage,
one should cut off the flowers of Māra here and go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
He who, having understood that there is no essence in states of existence, just like the flower of the udumbara tree,
is a bhikṣu who abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake casts off its old, withered skin.
He who completely cuts off passion, as one plucks a lotus flower from the water after diving in,
that monk leaves behind this shoreless world, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.
The monk who cuts off hatred without remainder, as one plucks a lotus flower from the water after diving into it— he indeed leaves this world behind, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.
He who cuts off delusion without remainder, like one diving into the water and plucking a lotus flower from its stalk—
he indeed, as a monk, abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.
He who cuts off pride without remainder, like one diving into the water and plucking a lotus flower from its stalk—
he indeed, as a monk, abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who cuts off greed without remainder, like one diving into the water and plucking a lotus flower from its stalk— he indeed leaves this world behind, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who cuts off craving entirely, like one who has plunged into the water and plucked a lotus flower from its root— he indeed leaves this world behind, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.
Chapter 19: The Chapter on Horses Just as a noble horse, when touched by the whip, becomes alert and exerts itself, so too should one who is ardent practice with vigilance.
One who is faithful, endowed with the virtues of moral discipline, concentrated, and skilled in the discernment of the Dharma—[being thus touched by the whip of the Teacher]—should likewise proceed.
Having conquered the senses and being endowed with the power of patience, he abandons all states of existence without exception.

Just as a noble horse, when struck by the whip, becomes alert and exerts itself, so too should one who is ardent practice with vigilance. One who is faithful, endowed with the virtues of moral conduct, concentrated, and skilled in the determination of the Dharma—
possessed of both knowledge and conduct, mindful, and a protector— abandons all suffering.
For one whose senses have attained equanimity, like a horse well-tamed by a charioteer,
even the gods always envy him who has abandoned faults and is free from outflows.
Vigilant among the heedless, wide awake while others sleep,
like a weak horse leaving behind a noble steed, he goes toward the wise one.
For the man who practices modesty, who is wise and well-composed, [attains the highest state].
For he abandons all evil, just as a well-trained horse avoids the whip.
The self-controlled indeed goes to the assembly; the king mounts the self-controlled.
The self-controlled man who endures harsh speech is the best among men.
For he would be like one who could tame a wild horse, a noble thoroughbred, or a Sindhu steed.
Or even a great elephant, a noble tusker; yet a tamed self is better than that.
And rather than one who might tame here a young mule, or even a noble Saindhava horse,
or a great elephant, better is he who has tamed himself.
For one does not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
rather, with a self well-tamed, one swiftly attains peace.
For one who is self-tamed and tamed does not reach that state by means of that vehicle which he travels by means of his own well-tamed self.
And compared to one who might here tame a young mule, or even a noble horse from Sindh, or a great elephant, the self-tamed person is superior to them all.
For one does not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
rather, by means of a well-tamed self, one abandons all miserable destinies.
For one could not reach that state by means of that vehicle as effectively as one who,
through his own well-tamed self, causes all miserable rebirths to cease.
And better than one who would here tame a young mule, or even a noble Saindhava horse, or a great elephant, is he who tames himself.
For one does not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
rather, with one's own self well-tamed, one cuts through all bondage.
For one could not reach that state by means of that vehicle as well as one who,
having thoroughly tamed himself, cuts through every bond.
And better than one who would here tame a young mule, or even a noble Saindhava horse, or a great elephant, is he who tames himself.
For one does not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
rather, it is by means of a well-tamed self that one is liberated from all suffering.
For one could not reach that state by means of that vehicle as well as one who,
through their own well-tamed self, is liberated from all suffering.
And better than one who would here tame a young mule, or even a noble Saindhava horse, or a great elephant, is he who tames himself.
For one could not reach that state by means of that vehicle as well as one reaches every excellence by means of a self that is thoroughly subdued.
And better than one who would here tame a young mule, or even a noble Saindhava horse, or a great elephant, is he who tames himself.
For one does not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
indeed, it is by means of a well-tamed self that one draws near to nirvana itself.
For one could not reach that state by means of that vehicle;
rather, it is by means of oneself being well-tamed that one is near to Nirvana itself.
One should tame oneself alone, as a charioteer tames a noble horse;
for by means of a well-tamed self, one who possesses mindfulness reaches the further shore of suffering.
For oneself alone is one's own protector; oneself is the refuge of oneself.
Therefore, restrain yourself as a charioteer restrains a noble horse.
One should abandon anger and cast off pride; one should transcend all fetters.
For him who is unattached to name and form, who possesses nothing, no attachments follow after.
One should abandon anger as soon as it arises; one should restrain passion once it has been born;
the wise person should utterly renounce ignorance through the realization of truth, thereby attaining happiness.
Having slain anger, one sleeps in peace; having slain anger, one does not grieve.
O monks, the Noble Ones praise the destruction of anger, which has poison as its root and sweetness as its destroyer; and having slain it, one does not grieve.
But when one who is angry approves of an evil deed as if it were a good one,
he later suffers like one who has touched fire once his anger has subsided.
One who is shameless, lacking in dread of blame, devoid of vows, and prone to anger—
for one thus overcome by wrath, there is no island of refuge whatsoever here in this world.
One who lacks shame and has no sense of dread, who is wrathful and devoid of vows—
when overcome by anger, there is no island of refuge whatsoever for such a person.
For the strength of one whose strength is found in anger is actually weakness;
for one who is angry and devoid of Dharma, right practice does not exist.
But when one who is powerful endures the harm of the weak, they call that the supreme patience; for the weak person always endures.
When one who is powerful toward others endures those who are weak, they call that the supreme patience; for the weak person always endures.
When one who is indeed powerful endures being reviled by others, they call that the supreme patience; whereas the weak person always forgives out of necessity.
He protects both himself and others from great danger who,
perceiving another to be enraged, himself remains calm in that situation.
He accomplishes the welfare of both himself and another who,
knowing the other to be angry, himself remains calm in that situation.
The fool, lacking discernment regarding the true nature of phenomena, considers him who acts for the benefit of both himself and others to be weak.
Indeed, the fool considers himself victorious when speaking harsh words;
but for him who endures such abuse,
victory is as constant as it is for the one who patiently bears the speech of his superior out of fear, the speech of his equal out of rivalry, and the speech of his inferior out of compassion.
The noble ones say that the ability to endure the speech of an inferior person is the highest form of patience in this world.
One who is angry should not speak words, whether in assemblies or in private;
for a man overcome by anger does not perceive his own true interest.
One should speak the truth, one should not become angry, and one should give even from what is little;
endowed with these three qualities, one goes to the presence of the gods.
For how could there be anger in one who is peaceful, self-controlled, and lives in equanimity?
For the wise one who is rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, there is no anger.
The sin belongs only to him who becomes angry in return when another is angry;
but he who remains unangered toward those who are angry shall win a battle difficult to conquer.
One should conquer anger with non-anger; one should conquer the wicked with goodness.
One should conquer the miser with generosity, and one should conquer the untruthful with truth.
How can there be anger in one who is not angry, who is self-controlled, and who lives in equanimity?
For one who is fully liberated through right understanding, anger does not exist.
Absence of anger and non-violence always abide among the noble;
whereas among sinful people, anger remains forever like a mountain.
But he who can hold back anger that has arisen here, like a runaway chariot, him I call a charioteer; any other is merely a holder of reins.
20. Summary verse:
The ascetic, the path, hospitality, malice, mindfulness, miscellaneous matters, water, flowers, and the horse; together with anger, these are the ten.
I am the Tathāgata, the one who overcomes all, and the all-knowing; I am forever unstained by any phenomena.
Having abandoned everything and being liberated from all fear, having realized this for myself, whom should I point to [as my teacher]?

Whom indeed should I point out [as my teacher], for I am peerless and incomparable; having myself realized awakening, the Tathāgata, the teacher of gods and humans, has attained omniscience and is endowed with the powers.
For I am indeed the Arhat in the worlds; I am the unsurpassed one in the worlds; and among the worlds including the gods, O Māra, I am the Conqueror who has overcome you.
I have no teacher at all, nor is there anyone equal to me;
I am the sole perfectly awakened one in this world, having attained supreme enlightenment.
Those like me who have attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) are to be known as Jinas;
I have conquered all unwholesome states (pāpakā dharmāḥ), therefore, O Upagā, I am a Jina.
I shall go to Vārāṇasī; I shall beat the drum of the Deathless;
I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dharma, which has never been turned before in the worlds.
For the wise do not manifest themselves after having understood the course of the world; those sages of tranquil mind point out the stainless state.
Here the great heroes, the Tathāgatas, roar with the true Dharma; who that possesses discernment would feel envy toward those roaring with the Dharma?
The wise who are dedicated to meditation, who delight in renunciation and tranquility—
of those illustrious Buddhas, even the gods always feel envy.
Both gods and humans long for those illustrious, perfectly awakened ones who possess such wisdom and bear their final bodies.
Those who were the perfectly awakened ones of the past, those who are the Buddhas of the future,
and he who is the perfectly awakened one at present— the destroyer of the sorrow of many.
All the Buddhas have taught, are teaching, and will continue to teach the True Dharma as their teacher; this is the natural law among Buddhas.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare and aspires to greatness in this world should hold the true Dharma in high esteem, remembering the teaching of the Buddha.
Those men who indeed do not have faith in the teaching of the Buddha will meet with calamity, like merchants among ogresses.
But those people who always have faith in the teaching of the Buddha will proceed in safety,
just as merchants [proceed] by means of the Vālāha horse.
Two thoughts indeed frequently arise here concerning the Tathāgata, the Buddha, the self-existent one:
that he is secure and likewise devoted to solitude, the great seer who dispels darkness and has reached the further shore.

And that Noble One has attained complete mastery; he is supreme over the universe, liberated from all fear, with craving abandoned, stainless, and free from longing, as he gazes upon sentient beings for their welfare.
Just as one standing on the summit of a mountain might see the multitude of people all around,
even so did that wise one, free from sorrow, having ascended the palace made of Dharma with his all-seeing eye, behold this multitude overcome by grief, overwhelmed by birth and old age.
22. The Chapter on Learning:
It is good to have learning, good to have well-practiced conduct, and good as well to be homeless; going forth and following the life of a recluse are conducive to the state of a śramaṇa.
Fools here move about as if they were immortal, not understanding;
but for those who know the true Dharma, life is like the night of one who is afflicted.
For just as one with sight, having entered a well-covered house that is filled with darkness, does not see the forms that are present there;
In the same way, even a man here who is always possessed of knowledge does not understand virtuous or evil phenomena without having heard them.
Just as one with sight perceives forms by means of a lamp,
so too, having heard, one discerns phenomena that are wholesome and unwholesome.
Having heard the teachings, one understands them; having heard them, one does not practice evil;
having heard them, one avoids what is harmful; and having heard them, one attains nirvāṇa.
Even if one is very learned, if one is not concentrated in moral conduct, people censure them for their lack of virtue; thus, their learning does not bear fruit.
Even if one has heard little, if they are well-composed in their moral conduct,
people praise them for their virtue, and learning will come to them.
Even if one has little learning, if they are undisciplined in their ethical conduct,
people censure them on both counts, and their vow does not succeed.
Even if one is very learned and well-composed in moral virtues,
people praise him on both counts, and his vow becomes successful.
