Who would be fit to revile one who is deeply learned, upholder of the Dharma, wise, and always composed, like a necklace made of pure gold from the Jambū river?
Those people who measure me by my form, and those who follow after my voice,
being under the sway of desire and passion, do not truly know me.
Those people who judge me by my form and follow me by my voice,
being under the sway of desire and passion, do not know me.
One who does not know the internal, but perceives only the external,
seeing only external fruits, is indeed led away by mere sound.
But one who understands the internal yet does not see the external,
and who perceives only the internal fruit, is indeed led away by mere sound.
One who does not know the internal and does not see the external,
seeing no fruit in either— such a person is indeed led away by mere sound.
He understands the internal and perceives the external;
possessing wisdom regarding liberation, he is indeed not led away by mere sound.
One hears much with the ear and sees much with the eye;
however, a wise person ought not to place faith in everything seen or heard.
Much is heard with the ear, and much is seen with the eye;
a wise person ought not to place faith in everything that has been seen or heard.
Well-spoken words have discernment as their essence, and knowledge and learning have meditative concentration as their essence.
That man who is reckless and heedless gains neither the great purpose of discernment nor the value of his learning.

But those noble ones who delight in the Dharma proclaimed by the Sage, and who then practice according to what they have said, range within the domain of patience, gentleness, and meditative concentration; they have attained the very essence of both learning and wisdom.
23. Chapter on the Self:
A śramaṇa should train in well-spoken words and in attendance upon [the teacher];
in sitting alone in seclusion and in the calming of the mind.
With unwearied mind, he should find delight in a single seat, a single bed, and a solitary course; alone, he should always dwell in the forests, delighting in the Self alone.
He who should conquer a thousand times a thousand enemies in battle,
and he who should conquer himself alone— that latter battle is indeed difficult to win.
For one's own self conquered is better than these other creatures—
for a man who has subdued himself and always conducts himself with restraint.
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor Māra together with the brahmins, can achieve a victory over one who has been conquered; such is the case for the wise bhikṣu.
One should first establish oneself in what is appropriate;
thereafter, one may instruct others, just as one would oneself.
One should first establish oneself in what is appropriate, and only then instruct others; thus the wise person will not come to suffer.
One should indeed shape oneself in such a way that one may instruct another;
for my own self is always well-tamed, though it is indeed very difficult to tame.
One should indeed act toward oneself as one would instruct another;
for the self has been constantly tamed by me, and the person who has tamed their own self is truly wise.
One should not sacrifice one's own welfare for the sake of another, however great that other's interest may be;
having recognized one's own welfare as supreme, one should be devoted to one's own self-interest.
But the self is indeed the master of the self; for who else could be the master?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person gains a master.
But here, the self is the master of the self; for who else could be the master?
Indeed, by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains their goal.
But here, the self is the master of the self; for what other master could there be?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains the Dharma.
But here, the self is the lord of the self; for what other lord could there be?
Indeed, by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains glory.
But here, the self is the master of the self; for what other master could there be?
Indeed, by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains renown.
But here, the self is the master of the self; what other master could there possibly be?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains happiness.
But here, the self is the lord of the self; for what other lord could there be?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven.
But the self is indeed the master of the self; for what other master could there be? For by means of a well-tamed self, one is established in heaven for a long time.
But here, the self is the lord of the self; for what other lord could there be?
Indeed, by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains wisdom.
But the self is indeed the master of the self; for who else could be the master?
Indeed, with a well-tamed self, one shines resplendent among one's kinsmen.
But the self is indeed the lord of the self; what other lord could there possibly be?
For with a well-tamed self, one does not grieve in the midst of grief.
But here, the self is the master of the self; for what other master could there be?
For with a well-subdued self, one cuts through all bonds.
But here, the self is the master of the self; for what other master could there be?
For by means of a well-tamed self, one abandons all miserable rebirths.
But the self is indeed the master of the self; for who else could be the master? Indeed, by means of a well-tamed self, one is liberated from all suffering.
But here, the self is indeed the master of the self; for what other master could there be? For by means of a well-tamed self, one is indeed close to nirvana.
24. The Section on Repetition (Peyālavarga):
Even if one were to recite a hundred verses composed of meaningless words, a single meaningful word is better, hearing which one attains tranquility.
Better than reciting a hundred verses composed of unrighteous words is a single word of Dharma, hearing which one attains peace.
Better than living for a hundred years with immoral conduct and an unconcentrated mind is a single day lived by one who is virtuous and pure.
Better than living for a hundred years with poor wisdom and an unconcentrated mind is a single day's life of one who is wise and constantly meditative.
Better than living for a hundred years as one who is indolent and lacking in vigor is a single day lived by one who exerts firm energy.
Better is life for a single day for one who perceives the rise and fall [of phenomena], than to live for a hundred years without perceiving their rise and fall.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the destruction of suffering is a single day of life for one who sees the destruction of suffering.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the destruction of the outflows is a single day of life for one who sees the destruction of the outflows.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the immovable state is a single day's life of one who beholds the immovable state.
Better than living for a hundred years without beholding the imperishable state is a single day's life of one who beholds the imperishable state.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the stainless state is to live for a single day while seeing the stainless state.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the stainless state is a single day's life of one who beholds the stainless state.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the difficult-to-behold state is to live for a single day seeing the difficult-to-behold state.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the supreme state is to live for a single day while beholding the supreme state.
Better than living for a hundred years without beholding the immortal state is a single day's life of one who beholds the immortal state.
Whether one should tend the sacrificial fire in the forest for a full hundred years,
or whether one who has cultivated the self should honor [the Buddha] for even a moment— the latter act of honoring is superior; that hundred-year sacrifice is not equal to it.
If one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of the merit of serene faith in the Dharma.
If one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the faith placed in the Sangha.
If one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the merit of serene confidence in ethical discipline.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
it would not be worth a sixteenth part of a mind of loving-kindness.
If one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that act does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of compassion for sentient beings.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of compassion for living beings.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of compassion for living beings.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the well-expounded Dharma.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
One who might conquer [in battle] with a thousand [men] month after month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of serene confidence in the Dharma.
Even if one were to sacrifice a thousand [coins] every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the faith placed in the Saṅgha.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of serene confidence in moral discipline.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [pieces of gold] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of one whose mind is friendly.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the compassion shown toward sentient beings.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the compassion shown toward living beings.
Even if one were to sacrifice a thousand [times] every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of compassion toward living beings.
He who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the well-expounded Dharma.

Whatever sacrifice or oblation one who seeks merit performs in this world for an entire year, all of that does not equal even a fourth part of the merit gained from showing reverence to those who walk uprightly; indeed, such reverence is superior.
25. A wise person should not form friendship with those who lack faith, the miserly, the slanderous, or those who delight in worldly power; for association with the wicked is indeed evil.

A wise person should cultivate friendship with those who are faithful, amiable, virtuous, and learned; for association with the good is auspicious. One should not associate with an evil friend, nor should one associate with a base person.
One should associate with a virtuous friend; one should associate with a supreme person.
Truly, men should be served who are rich in learning and contemplative of their station;
for by hearing their well-spoken words, one attains excellence even without them.
A man who serves the base declines, but he who serves his equal certainly does not decline;
for by approaching the superior, one attains excellence. Therefore, in this world, one should devote oneself to the superior.
For he who constantly serves those who are superior— those most excellent through wisdom, virtue, and tranquility— attains what is truly beneficial.
Just as a man who ties putrid fish to the tip of a blade of kusha grass causes even that kusha grass to emit a foul odor, so too does one who associates with the wicked become tainted by their evil.
Just as a man who wraps tagara with a leaf of the palāśa tree makes even those leaves fragrant, so too does association with the virtuous always produce goodness.
Even if one does not commit evil deeds oneself, by associating with one who commits them,
one becomes suspicious of evil and one's own ill-repute increases.
For a wicked person, by associating with others, defiles them through that contact;
like an arrow smeared with poison, it taints those unsmearable feathers in the quiver.
Therefore, out of fear of such defilement, a wise man should never become a friend of the wicked.
Whatever kind of friend one makes and whatever kind of person one serves, before long one becomes like them, for one's service conforms to that of the one served.
Therefore, having seen the ripening of his own fruit within the very vessel,
the wise man should not serve the wicked, but should serve the virtuous.
Even if a fool attends upon the wise for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dharma, just as a ladle cannot taste the flavor of the soup.
Even for a moment, the wise person who attends upon the learned understands the Dharma,
just as the tongue perceives the flavors of soup.
Even if a fool attends upon the wise for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dharma, for he lacks wisdom.
Even for a moment, one who possesses wisdom attends upon the learned;
he indeed understands the Dharma, for wisdom exists within him.
Even if a fool attends upon the wise for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Even for a moment, one who possesses wisdom attends upon the learned;
he indeed understands the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Awakened One.
A single meaningful word spoken by a wise person brings about benefit; however, even everything spoken by the Buddha may not lead to the welfare of a fool.
The fool does not comprehend a single step even with a thousand steps;
the wise man, by means of a single step, finds a hundred steps.
A wise person who is an enemy is better than a compassionate fool;
for a fool, when he shows compassion, drags one down into the hells.
He who knows "I am a fool" is a wise man;
but the fool who considers himself wise is called a fool indeed.
Whatever a fool may praise and whatever a wise man may censure—
the censure of the wise is superior, but not the praise of a fool.
One should not look upon a fool, nor hear him, nor dwell with him;
for dwelling with fools is painful in every respect, just like dwelling with an enemy. But dwelling with the wise is pleasant, like a reunion with kinsmen.
One should attend upon one who is steadfast, wise, virtuous, and learned—one who is a leader endowed with speed, just as the hosts of stars attend upon the moon.
26. The Chapter on Nirvana.
Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its own shell, so should one draw back the thoughts of the self;
for, being independent, not harming others, and having attained final nirvana, one should not disparage anyone.
Patience is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare that endurance is the highest Nirvana. For one who harms others is not a renunciant, nor does one who oppresses others truly become a Shramana.
Do not speak harshly to anyone; for when addressed thus, they respond in kind. Indeed, angry words lead to suffering, as they surely touch upon a counter-reprisal.
Since you always strike at yourself like a bronze gong being beaten,
you will indeed experience for a long time the cycle of birth and death.
Yet you do not stir yourself, like a gong that has not been struck;
you have reached Nirvana, for no agitation remains within you.
Health is the supreme gain; contentment is the supreme wealth;
trust is the supreme friend; and Nirvana is the supreme happiness.
Hunger is the supreme among diseases, and conditioned formations are indeed suffering;
knowing this as it truly is, one should be intent upon Nirvana as the highest goal.
Few go to a happy rebirth; many go to an unhappy rebirth.
Having known this as it truly is, one should become one for whom nirvana is supreme.
With cause they go to a happy destination; with cause they go to an evil destination;
with cause they attain final nirvana; for thus it is with a cause.
The forest is the refuge of wild animals; the sky is the refuge of birds;
Dharma is the refuge of those who possess discernment; but Nirvana is the refuge of Arhats.
...one should not dwell with them.
For it is not possible for one who is lacking in vigor, who is dull-witted, and who is ignorant,
to attain Nirvana— the tearing asunder of all fetters.
...therefore, [be] restrained regarding sensual pleasures.
Bury this boat of the monk; once buried, it will become light.
Having abandoned both passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain Nirvāṇa.
It did not exist before, nor did it exist after that; indeed, it did not exist before, nor will it exist, nor is it found at present.
For one who penetrates the truth that is difficult to see and immovable— the well-seen—
and who perceives the destruction of craving, the end of suffering is declared.
Having cut off craving and stilled all passion here, being fully concentrated,
and having dried up the rivers, one is said to have reached the end of suffering.
Having broken through the body and perception, and having stilled sensation, one attains the disappearance of consciousness; this is declared to be the end of suffering.
When the seen is merely seen, and the heard is merely heard, and likewise when the thought is merely thought and the known is merely known, the end of suffering is declared.
For one who understands "this is suffering" and "this is the origin of suffering," the cessation of all evil is declared to be the end of suffering.
Abstention from meat, abstention from fermented grain, and total abstinence everywhere— this complete desisting from all evil is declared to be the end of suffering.
For one who is non-dependent, there is here immovability and pliancy;
there is neither going nor passing away, and this is declared to be the end of suffering.
When the unborn exists, one should always speak of the escape from the born;
and by perceiving the unconditioned, one is liberated from the conditioned.
That which is born, come into being, arisen, created, conditioned, unstable,
a confluence of old age and death, subject to deception and dissolution,
originating from the flow of nutriment— that is not fit to be rejoiced in.
Its escape is peace, a state beyond the reach of discursive thought;
it is the cessation of all phenomena of suffering, the blissful stilling of conditioned formations.
I recall a state where no being is found,
neither space nor consciousness, neither sun nor moon.
There is neither non-coming nor going, neither birth nor death;
that which is without support and without objective basis is called the end of suffering.
Where neither water nor earth, nor fire nor wind penetrates,
there the white [lights] do not shine, and darkness is not found there.
There the moon does not shine, nor indeed is the sun made manifest; rather,
as the sage here perceives through the self the silence of the self,
he is then liberated from all suffering, both from form and from the formless.
Having reached the ultimate goal, you are indeed free from fear, neither boastful nor remorseful; be the one who cuts away the thorns of existence—this is your final embodiment.
For this is the supreme consummation, the peaceful, unsurpassed state;
it is the exhaustion of all signs, the immutable state of giving.

The Sage, delighting in the inner self and composed in concentration, cast off existence and its formative forces— both the similar and the dissimilar— as he shattered the shell born of the egg, as it were.
All giving is surpassed by the gift of Dharma; all delight is surpassed by delight in the Dharma;
all strength is surpassed by the strength of patience; and the cessation of all craving surpasses all happiness.
The gift of Dharma surpasses all gifts; the delight in Dharma surpasses all delights;
the power of patience surpasses all powers; and the destruction of craving surpasses all happiness.
27. O you who see, the faults of others are easy to perceive, but one's own faults are difficult to see;
for one person winnows away the faults of another like chaff.
For those who look for the faults of others and are constantly preoccupied with thoughts of disparagement, unwholesome qualities increase; for they are far from the vision of the Dharma.
Life would be easy for one who is shameless, as bold as a crow, as greedy as a vulture, impetuous, and arrogant; yet, such a life is lived here in a state of affliction.
But for one who possesses a sense of shame, who is ever seeking purity, who is well-restrained, unassuming, pure in livelihood, and discerning, life here is indeed difficult to lead.
For this world has become blind; here, for one who sees clearly, it is but a narrow space.
Like a bird released from a net, he rejoices only briefly in the heavens.
The world, bound by deception, appears as if it were real;
fools, bound by acquisitions and enveloped in darkness, see the non-existent as existent. To one who sees clearly, however, nothing at all exists.
Mortals are driven by the sense of "I" and bound to the actions of others;
some do not understand this, for they do not see it as a thorn piercing them.
But having extracted this thorn while observing that to which living beings are attached and intent—
thinking "I do it"— one should not harm him, thinking "another does it," nor should one harm him, thinking "I am doing it."
For this world is possessed by pride, always remains attached to pride,
and being agitated by various views, it does not transcend saṃsāra.
That which has been attained and that which is yet to be attained—this dyad is strewn with passion.
Knowing this to be a state of affliction, the wise man, being composed, should abandon it.
Those beings who have the training as their essence, who live by the sacred life and live by celibacy,
and who delight in service— this alone is proclaimed as the one extreme.
"Desires should be enjoyed when pure; no fault is found in them. Such is the view of the foolish; this is proclaimed as the second extreme.
Fools, not understanding these two extremes, remain submerged in them;
others, however, run beyond them; but the one with vision perceives them both.
Having understood these two extremes, those who are wise do not exist [as entities] therein; nor do they conceive themselves by means of that [existence], for no path leading back to them is found.
Just as one might view a bubble, just as one might view a mirage—
so indeed perceiving the world, one does not see the King of Death.
Just as one might view a bubble, just as one might view a mirage—
so indeed regarding the body, one does not see the King of Death.
Behold this body, ever variegated like a king’s chariot,
wherein fools are utterly deluded, yet for those who possess true knowledge, there is no attachment.
Behold this body, ever variegated like a king’s chariot;
therein the foolish despair, but the wise become dispassionate.
Behold this body, ever variegated like a king’s chariot,
wherein fools sink down like an old ox in the mud.
Behold this body, ever variegated like a king’s chariot;
herein the foolish are utterly deluded, but the wise become dispassionate. Behold this painted image, designated as "body," which is devoid of disease.
He who is afflicted by the intention for theft has no stable state.
...there is no attachment for those who possess true knowledge.
Behold the image fashioned with variegated jewels and earrings;
it is sufficient for the delusion of a child, but not for those seeking the further shore.
Behold the image fashioned by a painter, as well as those made of jewels and earrings; they are sufficient to delude a child, but the wise man becomes dispassionate toward them.
With his limbs anointed with perfume and his feet stained with red ochre,
this is sufficient to delude the fool, but not those who seek the further shore.
With his body anointed with fragrance and his feet stained with red ochre—this is sufficient to delude a fool; herein the wise man becomes dispassionate.
Behold this painted image, adorned with jewels and earrings; it is enough to delude a child... Behold this painted image, adorned with jewels and earrings.
Enough for the delusion of the fool...
her hair is arranged in eight braids and her eyes are adorned with collyrium;
enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for those seeking the further shore.
The hair is arranged in eight rows and the eyes are adorned with collyrium;
this is sufficient to delude a fool, but the wise man becomes dispassionate toward it.
Enough with deluding the fool, for whom there is no stable abiding.
Attachment is sufficient for the delusion of a fool; it does not exist for those who possess true knowledge.
Like a fresh, variegated collyrium box, this putrid body is indeed adorned;
it is sufficient for the delusion of the fool, but not for those seeking the further shore.
Like a new, variegated ointment-box, this putrid body is indeed adorned;
it is sufficient to delude the fool, but the wise person becomes dispassionate toward it.
With his body anointed with perfume and his feet stained with red ochre,
this is enough to delude a fool who possesses no stable foundation.
With his body anointed with perfume and his feet stained with red ochre, this is enough to delude a fool; for those who possess true knowledge, there is no attachment.
Like a new, variegated collyrium box, this putrid body is indeed adorned;
it is sufficient for the delusion of a fool, for whom there is no permanent stability.
Like a new, variegated collyrium-box, this putrid body is indeed adorned;
it is sufficient for the delusion of a fool, but for those who understand, there is no attachment.
For those fools who are constantly attached to sensual pleasures and do not perceive the fault in fetters will never,
while clinging to the attachment of fetters, cross over the vast and great flood.

Free from passion above, below, and on all sides, and not perceiving "I am this," one who is thus liberated indeed crosses over the flood in this world— that which was never crossed before— for the sake of non-rebirth.
Behold this person who, though liberated by those seeking nirvāṇa and released from the forest, runs back to the very forest; though freed from bondage, he runs toward bondage itself.
With beautiful parts, covered in white, the chariot moves with a single wheel; its parts are blue. Behold it approaching—flawless, with its yoke severed and free from bonds.
Driven by fear, many people go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves, trees, and sacred shrines.
For this is not a secure refuge; this is not the supreme refuge.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
when he perceives the Four Noble Truths with wisdom—
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
For this indeed is the secure refuge; this is the supreme refuge.
Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
One who sees sees by means of seeing; one who does not see also sees.
One who does not see sees, but neither one who sees nor one who does not see sees.
Indeed, the difference between contemplation and vision is stated here;
just as there is no joining of day with nights, so too there is no joining of those two.
If one contemplates, one does not see; yet if one sees, one does not contemplate.
This one who sees does not contemplate, but while contemplating, one never sees.
What is it that one who sees does not perceive? What is it that one who does not see does not perceive? When what exists is there perception, and when what does not exist is there no perception?
That which he does not see as suffering, failing to see it as such, he perceives as the self;
but seeing suffering exactly as it is, he constantly perceives that "this is the self."
Enveloped by which ordinary people do not see that conditioned phenomena are suffering;
when that exists, there is non-observation, and when it has ceased, there is the cessation of non-observation.
28. Chapter on Evil: The non-doing of all evil, the undertaking of what is wholesome, and the complete purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddha.
Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not created through self-restraint.
The virtuous person abandons evil; but through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, there is nirvana.
Whether wandering with others or always alone,
the wise one who knows the truth abandons evil, just as a crane leaves behind water mixed with milk.
Having seen the peril in the world and having known the Dharma that is free from affliction,
the noble one does not delight in evil, nor does the evil-doer delight in what is auspicious.
Having known the flavor of seclusion and the flavor of tranquility,
one becomes free from fever and free from evil, drinking the flavor of the joy of the Dharma.
But for one whose mind is not leaking away, whose consciousness is not bound,
and who has abandoned both merit and evil, there is no fear of an unfortunate rebirth.
One should always attend upon such a wise person who restrains others, speaks with authority, perceives what is blameworthy, and subdues the disputant;
for one who attends upon such a person, there arises spiritual welfare and not evil.
Truly peaceful, restrained, speaking little, and free from agitation,
he shakes off evil states just as the wind shakes the leaves from a tree.
For the evil that is directed against a man who is uncorrupted, pure, and eternally free from blemish,
falls back upon that very fool, just as dust thrown against the wind returns to the thrower.
Whatever a person does, that indeed he perceives within himself: the doer of good sees what is good, and the doer of evil sees what is evil.
For when evil is committed by oneself, one is always afflicted by oneself;
but when evil is not committed by oneself, one is purified by oneself alone.
One person cannot purify another's own impure mind;
rather, that evil crushes him, just as a diamond shatters a stone.
Just as one with sight would avoid treacherous places,
so should a wise person living in this world avoid all evils.
Just as a merchant on a perilous road with little wealth and great riches,
or one who desires life while facing poison, would avoid evils, so should one avoid sinful deeds.
If there should be no wound on his hand, he may hold the poison with his hand;
for poison does not enter that which is unwounded, and there is no sin for one who commits no evil.
For things that are unwholesome and detrimental to oneself are indeed easy to do;
but that which is truly beneficial and salutary is indeed extremely difficult to accomplish.
It is easy for the virtuous to do what is virtuous; it is difficult for the wicked to do what is virtuous.
It is easy for the wicked to do what is wicked; it is difficult for the noble to do what is wicked.
The fool thinks it is like honey as long as the evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, then he encounters suffering.
Even a wicked person sees what is auspicious as long as his evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, then he perceives evils.
Even a good person sees evil as long as his goodness has not ripened; but when his goodness ripens, then he beholds auspicious things.
If a person should commit a sin, he should not do it again and again;
one should not take pleasure in that, for the accumulation of sin is suffering.
But a person should perform merit, and he should do it again and again.
In this regard, one should cultivate aspiration; the accumulation of merit is blissful.
One should hasten toward what is auspicious and restrain the mind from evil. For the mind of one who performs merit sluggishly delights in sinful things. (The pair).
Even a small evil deed always leads to suffering in the future;
it results in great misfortune, just as poison that has entered the stomach.
Even a small amount of merit performed brings happiness in the next world;
it always leads to great benefit, just like the accumulation of grain.
For he who inflicts punishment upon those who do not deserve it, and who offends against those who are innocent,
will swiftly fall into one of ten states.
Whether it be the loss of kinsmen, the exhaustion of enjoyments,
misfortune from the king, or even a terrible accusation.
Whether it be bitter sensation, or even the breaking apart of the body,
or even harsh affliction, or even mental distraction.
Or else, fire will burn his very houses in every way;
moreover, upon the dissolution of the body, the unwise man shall go to the tenth miserable destiny.
When an evil deed has been committed, one should not feel secure; whether it was done long ago or far away, one should not feel secure;
even if done in secret, one should not feel secure—for there is its ripening—and thus one should never feel secure.
When merit has been performed here, one may take heart; even when it was performed long ago or far back in time, one may take heart;
even when it was performed in secret, one may take heart; and one may take heart thinking, "There is its ripening."
When evil has been committed, one indeed grieves; even when it was committed long ago or far away, one grieves;
even when it was committed in secret, one grieves, thinking: "There is its ripening"—thus one grieves.
When merit has been performed, one indeed rejoices; even when it was performed long ago or performed far away, one rejoices;
and even when it was performed in secret, one rejoices, thinking, "There is its ripening," and thus one rejoices.
Here one grieves, after death one grieves; for the doer of evil grieves in both places.
Indeed, he grieves and laments upon seeing his own defiled deed.
One rejoices here, one rejoices after passing away; indeed, the one who has performed merit rejoices in both places.
For he rejoices and exults upon seeing his own purified action.
When evil has been committed, one indeed grieves; one grieves even when it was done long ago or far away;
one grieves even when done in secret; and having fallen into a miserable rebirth, one grieves all the more.
When merit has been performed, one rejoices; even when it was performed long ago or far away, one rejoices;
even when it was performed in secret, one rejoices; and having attained a good rebirth, one rejoices all the more.
Indeed, one rejoices when merit has been performed; one rejoices even when it was performed long ago or at a great distance;
one rejoices even when it was performed in secret; and having attained a good rebirth, one rejoices all the more.
Whether a sin has been committed or merit has been performed, one who adopts unrighteousness and abandons the Dharma—
a doer of evil deeds— fears death here like a man with a broken boat in the middle of the water.
Indeed, one who has performed merit and avoided evil, and who practices the ancient dharma of the virtuous,
never fears death at all, just as those crossing in a sturdy boat have no fear of the water.
29. That worm shines only so long as the sun has not arisen;
but once the sun, the illuminator, has risen, it becomes utterly dark and no longer shines.
Thus it was said by the logicians: "As long as the Tathāgata has not arisen, [it is so];
but when the world is illuminated by the Buddha, neither the logician nor his disciple shines."
Those who perceive the essential in the unessential, and the unessential in the essential,
do not attain the essential, for they dwell within the sphere of false conceptualization.
Having understood the essential through its essence and the non-essential through its lack of essence,
those whose range of activity is right intention attain the essential.
For they run hither and thither with the notion that this is the essence, taking up one new bond after another;
indeed, they fall like moths into a flame from the darkness, their minds fixed only upon what is seen and heard.
For whatever doubt there may be here, whether concerning this world or another, this shore or the further shore—
all that those who meditate cast off entirely, being ardent as they lead the holy life.
He who, being free from passion, shall put on the saffron robe, yet lacks self-control and gentleness— he does not deserve the saffron robe.
But he who has vomited out his impurities, who is well-composed in moral virtues, and who is endowed with self-control and gentleness— he indeed deserves the saffron robe.
He whose faults have been completely uprooted, severed like the head of a palmyra tree— he who has vomited out his defects, the wise one, is called "one of virtuous form."
A man does not become truly handsome merely by name, nor even by a fullness of complexion;
he may have a beautiful form but be deceitful, envious, and treacherous.
For not every man is recognized by his complexion or form, nor is he known by a fleeting glance;
yet those who are well-restrained here may move about this world with the outward marks of those who are unrestrained.

Some wander about with retinues, like counterfeit coins with incense-smoked centers, or like half-māṣas of iron covered in gold; yet they are inwardly impure while appearing beautiful on the outside. Such a person is drowsy, a great devourer, and rolls about sleeping day and night.
Like a great boar fattened on sacrificial offerings, he enters the womb again and again, slowly.
For a person who is always mindful, who knows the proper measure of food, and who possesses mindfulness, his painful sensations become slight; he ages slowly while preserving his life-force.

Passion overcomes one who constantly contemplates the beautiful, who is unrestrained in his senses, who lacks moderation in eating, and who is deficient in vigilance— just as the wind overthrows a weak tree.
Dwelling while contemplating the beautiful, with his sense-faculties unrestrained,
lacking moderation in food, lazy, and deficient in vigor—
passion indeed overcomes him, just as the wind overcomes a weak tree.
One who constantly perceives the beautiful, who does not restrain his sense faculties,
who lacks moderation in eating, and who is deficient in wakefulness—
hatred indeed overcomes him, just as the wind overthrows a weak tree.
Delighting constantly in the beautiful, with the senses unrestrained,
immoderate in eating, and deficient in wakefulness— delusion surely overcomes such a person, as the wind strikes down a weak tree.
One who constantly contemplates the beautiful, who does not restrain his sense faculties,
who lacks moderation in eating, and who is deficient in wakefulness—
arrogance indeed overcomes him, just as the wind strikes down a weak tree.
One who constantly contemplates the beautiful, who is unrestrained in his senses,
who lacks moderation in eating, and who is deficient in wakefulness—
greed indeed overcomes him, just as the wind overcomes a weak tree.

Craving overcomes one who constantly contemplates the beautiful, who is unrestrained in the senses, who lacks moderation in food, and who is deficient in wakefulness— just as the wind overthrows a weak tree.

Passion does not overcome one who constantly contemplates the foul, who is well-restrained in his senses, who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is disciplined in wakefulness— just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.
Contemplating the foul, detached from the sense-faculties, well-restrained, moderate in eating, faithful, and possessing initiated vigor—
passion cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot shake a mountain of rock.

Hatred does not overcome one who constantly contemplates the foul, who is well-restrained in his senses, who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is disciplined in wakefulness— just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.

Delusion does not overcome one who constantly contemplates the foul, who is well-restrained in his senses, who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is disciplined in wakefulness— just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.

One who constantly contemplates the foul, whose senses are well-restrained, who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is disciplined in wakefulness— conceit cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.
One who constantly contemplates the foul, is well-restrained in the senses, knows moderation in food, and is disciplined in wakefulness—
greed cannot overcome such a person, just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.
One who constantly contemplates the foul, who is well-restrained in the senses,
who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is disciplined in wakefulness—
thirst cannot overcome such a person, just as the wind cannot shake a firm mountain.
The forests are delightful, yet people do not find pleasure therein;
those free from passion will rejoice here, but not those who seek after sensual desires.
Whether in a village or in a forest, whether in low ground or on high ground—
wherever the Arhats dwell, those regions are delightful.
The virtuous are revealed from afar, like the Himalaya mountain;
the wicked are not revealed at all, like arrows shot in the night.
One should dwell only with the virtuous, with the wise who contemplate the true meaning;
for through wisdom, one penetrates the great and profound meaning.

Like an elephant in battle, I endure harsh words as I do arrows shot from a bow, for the great mass of people is ill-behaved. And having seen fear in existence, I shall endure it, and furthermore, I shall see prosperity within existence.
Therefore, I do not delight in existence, nor do I find joy in non-existence.
The man who is faithless, ungrateful, and a breaker of agreements— he who is devoid of faith, whose opportunity is destroyed, and whose hope has been vomited out— he indeed is the Supreme Person.
Having slain his mother and father, a king, and two Vedic scholars;
having destroyed a kingdom along with its subjects, a Brahmin goes forth free from taint.

For those who have no accumulation, who have fully understood food, for whom emptiness, the signless, and solitude are the very sphere of activity— their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.

For those who have no accumulation, who have fully understood food, whose sphere of activity is emptiness, the signless, and solitude— their track is difficult to follow, like that of birds in the sky.

For those who have no accumulation, who have fully understood food, for whom emptiness, the signless, and concentration are their very domain— their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.

For those who have no accumulation, who have fully understood food, for whom emptiness, the signless, and concentration are their very domain— their path is as difficult to track as that of birds in the sky.

For those whose existence is completely exhausted and who do not rely upon the future limit, for whom emptiness, the signless, and solitude alone are the sphere of experience— their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.

For those whose existence is completely exhausted and who do not rely upon the future limit, for whom emptiness, the signless, and solitude are the very sphere of experience— their course is as difficult to trace as that of birds in the sky.

For those whose existence is completely exhausted and who do not rely on the future limit, for whom emptiness, the signless, and meditative concentration are the very range of experience— their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.
For those whose existence is completely exhausted and who do not rely upon the future limit,
for whom emptiness, the signless, and meditative concentration are their very domain— their course is as difficult to track as that of birds in the sky.
Few among those born of men are they who go to the further shore;
for the rest of these beings merely run along the near bank.
Those people, however, who perceive the Dharma within the Dharma that has been correctly proclaimed,
will go entirely beyond the domain of death.
For one who has traversed the path, who is free from sorrow, who is liberated, a protector,
and for whom all fetters have been abandoned, no fever exists.
The perilous path has been crossed; the underworld has been avoided;
one is liberated from both bonds and knots; and the entire poison of passion has been destroyed.
There is indeed no flood equal to desire; there is no seizure equal to hatred;
there is no net equal to delusion; there is no river equal to craving.
In space there is no footprint; there is no ascetic outside [the Dharma].
Fools delight in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), but the Tathāgatas are free from conceptual proliferation.
The fool is carried away by worldly attachments, while the wise man casts them off;
having cast off both divine and human attachments, the intelligent one attains liberation.
From union, existence arises; from separation, existence is destroyed.
Having understood these two paths—one leading to existence and the other to non-existence—the wise person should train therein so that they may transcend all unions.
It is better not to do an evil deed than to do it; for an evil deed burns later.
One grieves after having committed an evil deed, and one grieves when gone to an evil rebirth.
But a well-performed deed is better, having done which one does not regret;
having performed a good deed, one rejoices, and having gone to a happy destination, one rejoices.
When not speaking, the wise are not distinguished from fools; but when they speak, revealing the dustless state, they are known.
One should speak and illuminate the Dharma, and raise high the banner of the seers;
for the seers, out of reverence for the Dharma, always hold the banner of well-spoken words aloft.
They blame one who sits in silence; they blame one who speaks much;
and they blame even one who speaks little. There is no one in the worlds who is not blamed.
A person who is either exclusively censured or exclusively praised has never existed,
will not exist, nor is he found at present.
That which the wise praise after having investigated what is auspicious and inauspicious is declared to be true praise; however, that which is praised by the ignorant is not so.
Who could possibly find fault with one who is intelligent, endowed with good conduct, wise, and restrained in his virtues, like a necklace of pure Jāmbūnada gold?
Just as a solid mass of rock is not shaken by the wind,
so indeed are the wise not moved by blame or praise.
Who is worthy to revile that wise man who is liberated from bondage, whose root has no bark, whose leaves are gone, and likewise has no creepers?

Indeed, even the world with its gods does not recognize the Sage who wanders free from craving— he whose proliferation has ceased, whose continuity of existence is exhausted, and who has transcended the moat [of saṃsāra].
Whose victory is never surpassed, whose victory no one in the world can follow—he is the Buddha of infinite range; by what track will you lead him who is trackless?
For one who has no ensnaring, clinging craving that leads the world astray— that Buddha whose range is infinite and who is trackless— by what path will you lead him?
Who indeed would deserve to censure that wise man who is liberated from bondage— he whose root is not in the earth, and likewise has neither leaves nor creepers?
For him who possesses no ensnaring, clinging craving that leads one astray in the world—
that Buddha of infinite prowess, trackless one— by what path will you lead him?
He whose discursive thoughts have been shaken off and turned back within without remainder—
he, having transcended all attachment and every perception, goes beyond the state free from yoga to the one who has crossed over attachment.

Release it in front, release it behind, and release it in the middle; having reached the further shore of existence, with a mind free from attachment everywhere, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.
30. The Chapter on Happiness:
From victory, enmity is born; the defeated one sleeps in misery.
Having abandoned both victory and defeat, the one who is tranquil sleeps happily.
He who desires happiness for himself by inflicting suffering upon others,
being entangled in the bonds of enmity, is not liberated from suffering.
He who, seeking his own happiness, harms with violence those beings who desire happiness, shall indeed not obtain happiness.
He who, desiring his own happiness, does not harm beings who also desire happiness by means of punishment,
obtains happiness after death.
One should practice the Dharma well; one should not practice it poorly.
For he who practices the Dharma sleeps happily both in this world and in the next.
Dharma always protects the one who practices Dharma, just as a great umbrella protects from the rain during the rainy season.
This is the benefit when Dharma is well-practiced: the practitioner of Dharma does not go to an evil rebirth.
Dharma always protects the one who practices Dharma; Dharma, when well-practiced, bestows happiness.
This is the benefit of Dharma well-practiced: the practitioner of Dharma does not go to a state of woe.
Even if they are few, they conquer many through excellent arrangement; it is not the case that there is no arrangement.
Even if one gives only a little with faith, by that very act, one becomes happy in the next world.
They say that giving and battle are alike; these qualities do not belong to cowards.
For the occasion for giving is like the occasion for battle; they would be equal in terms of the collection of causes.
For I declare him to be more heroic than a hero who, having conquered hundreds of obstacles and overcome the enemy that is stinginess, gives a gift with an unattached mind;
for the ripening of his merits is blissful, and his intentions are fulfilled.
And he swiftly attains supreme peace, which is nirvāṇa.
For indeed, neither external calamities nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host are able to create obstacles for one who has performed meritorious deeds.
One who delights in the Dharma sleeps happily with a serene mind;
the wise and mindful person finds joy in the Dharma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.
Those whose minds delight in the Dharma, which leads to Nirvana through non-clinging,
and who are devoted to the foundations of mindfulness and the seven factors of enlightenment;
Those whose minds delight in the Dharma, finding liberation through non-clinging,
and who likewise delight in the bases of psychic power and the eightfold path;
They enjoy their alms-food with ease, and they wear their robes with ease;
their walking meditation is pleasant upon the mountains and in the caves.
For they have attained security and are happy; having realized nirvana in this very life, they have transcended all enmity and fear, and have crossed over the worldly attachment in the world.
But for one who is contented, who has heard the Dharma, and who sees clearly, solitude is happiness;
in this world, non-violence toward all living beings is happiness.
Detachment from the world is happiness, the transcendence of sensual desires is happiness, and the subduing of the conceit "I am" is indeed the supreme happiness.
Virtue is happiness until old age; happiness is faith firmly established;
happiness is speech devoted to the goal; and the non-doing of evil is happiness.
In this world, motherhood is happiness, and fatherhood is indeed happiness;
in this world, the state of being a recluse is happiness, and likewise, the state of being a brahmin is happiness.
The arising of a Buddha is happiness; the teaching of the Dharma is happiness;
the harmony of the Saṅgha is happiness; and the ascetic practice of those who are harmonious is happiness.
It is a joy to behold those who possess moral virtue; it is a joy to behold those who are deeply learned;
and it is a joy to behold Arhats who are fully liberated from rebirth.
Happy is the river with its excellent landing places; happy is the Victor who has conquered through the Dharma.

In every way, indeed, the Brahmin who has attained final liberation sleeps in peace—
he who is not defiled by sensual desires, who is utterly liberated, and who is free from outflows.
For having cut through all aspirations and removed the fever of the heart,
one who has attained peace of mind sleeps happily here, being thoroughly calmed.
He who, by relinquishing limited pleasure, perceives a vast happiness,
that wise man should renounce limited pleasure while clearly beholding the vast happiness.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever heavenly pleasure there may be,
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving.
Having indeed cast off the heavy burden, one should not take up another burden;
for the taking up of a burden is supreme suffering, while the casting off of a burden is happiness.
Having abandoned all craving, through the destruction of all fetters,
and having fully understood all substrata of existence, they do not come to renewed becoming.
When wealth has arisen, companions are happiness; merit is happiness at the time of the end of life;
contentment with whatever comes is happiness; and the cessation of all suffering is happiness.
Just as the course of a blazing fire struck by an iron hammer, which has been gradually extinguished, cannot be known; so it is with the one who has attained peace.
Thus, for those who are rightly liberated, who have crossed over the flood of the mire of sensual desires,

Like a water-born creature cast onto dry land, or one pulled from its element by a flood, the mind indeed quivers; O Māra, you must abandon your malice.
The mind wanders in various directions like the rays of the sun;

This mind is a vessel for the embryo; it is essence-less and invisible. I constantly instruct it so that it may not issue forth to my own detriment.
In the past, this mind wandered about wherever it wished, wherever it desired, and as it pleased;
now I restrain it thoroughly and fundamentally, just as one restrains a rutting elephant with a goad.
Having wandered through the cycle of many births again and again,

One who is not hateful should not act toward the hateful; nor should an enemy do what is beneficial for an enemy.
A mind wrongly directed would bring about its own ruin by itself.

The delight that comes from the fivefold musical ensemble is not like that which arises for one whose mind is one-pointed as they correctly discern the phenomena.

Placing right view at the forefront, knowing indeed the arising and passing away,

For the restraint of the mind is happiness; guard the mind and do not be negligent.

For the monk who has entered an empty dwelling, who is self-restrained, and who perceives the phenomena correctly, there arises a non-human delight in that empty dwelling.

I do not call one a brahmin by birth or origin from a mother;
O speaker, he is called a brahmin only if he possesses nothing. Indeed, I call him a brahmin who is without possessions and without grasping.
He who has committed no evil deed through body, speech, or mind, and who is well-restrained in these three ways— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who always speaks words that are neither harsh nor confusing, and by which no one would be provoked to anger— I indeed call him a brahmin.
He who, being free from malice, endures abuse, killing, and imprisonment— I call him indeed a brahmin, for he is endowed with the power of the vow of patience.
I call him indeed a brahmin who is free from anger, observant of vows, virtuous, deeply learned, self-controlled, and has reached the final state of the body.
One who is unmixed with both householders and renunciants, who wanders without a home and is content— him indeed I call a brahmin.
They do not rejoice when one has arrived, nor do they grieve when one departs;
liberated from attachment, like a victor in battle—I call him indeed a brahmin.
They do not rejoice when one has arrived, nor do they grieve when one departs;
him who is sorrowless, stainless, and peaceful, I call indeed a brahmin.
One who does not nourish others, who is self-knowing, self-controlled, and established in the essence;
whose taints are exhausted and whose faults have been vomited out—he indeed is remembered as a brahmin.
He for whom neither the far shore nor the near shore, nor both the far and near shores exist, and who has gone beyond all phenomena— him indeed I call a brahmin.
But he who takes nothing at all in this world— whether long or short, subtle or gross, auspicious or inauspicious— I call him indeed a Brahmin.
He for whom neither the further shore nor the near shore, nor both the further and near shores exist, who is unattached to the three worlds— him indeed I call a brahmin.
One who understands right here the destruction of his own suffering, who is free from passion and detached— I call him indeed a brahmin.
But he who is not smeared by either merit or demerits—
that one, free from sorrow, feverless, and peaceful, I indeed call a brahmin.
But he who has completely abandoned both merit and evil, as well as both attachments— to him, who has transcended attachment and is utterly detached, I indeed say, "He is a Brahmin."
He for whom there exists no attachment behind, in front, or even in the middle— stainless and liberated from bondage, him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who is not smeared by desires, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf or a mustard seed to the point of an awl— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who is not smeared by sins, like water on a lotus leaf or a mustard seed on the tip of an awl— him indeed I call a brahmin.
Like the moon— spotless, pure, serene, and indeed unclouded—
he who is not defiled by sensual desires, him I call a brahmin.
Like the moon— spotless, pure, serene, and indeed untroubled—
he who is not smeared by sins, him indeed I call a brahmin.
Like the moon—spotless, pure, serene, and indeed unclouded—be joyful; I declare that one whose [defilements] are utterly destroyed is indeed a brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin who is meditative, free from passion, one who has accomplished what was to be done, who is without outflows, whose taints are exhausted, and who is utterly detached.
I indeed call him a brahmin who possesses profound intelligence, who is rich in wisdom, who is skilled in discerning the right path from the wrong, and who has attained the supreme goal.

But whoever among men lives by the practice of begging, who is free from the sense of "mine," non-violent, ever steadfast, and observant of celibacy— who teaches the Dharma after having fully understood it— I indeed call him a brahmin.
Having abandoned all desires, he who wanders as a homeless renunciant,
freed from the influx of desire— I call him indeed a brahmin.
I call him indeed a Brāhmaṇa who has laid aside the rod toward all beings, both moving and stationary, and who does not kill living creatures.
He who is not defiled by desires, just as the sky is not defiled by mud or the moon by dust— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who is not smeared by sins, just as the sky is not defiled by mud or the moon by dust— he indeed, I call a Brāhmaṇa.
Like the sky is not defiled by mud, or like the moon by dust—
one whose attachment has completely perished, him indeed I call a brahmin.

One who is unopposed among those who are hostile, who remains composed toward those who wield the rod of punishment, and who is compassionate for the welfare of all beings— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He whose passion, hatred, pride, and hypocrisy have been cut away,
and who is not smeared by faults— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who has crossed over this difficult moat, the flood of saṃsāra;
who has reached the further shore, being meditative, unleadable, and beyond dispute; who is extinguished and free from clinging—I call him indeed a brahmin.
...him indeed I call a brahmin.
He for whom craving does not exist in this world nor in the next,
whose craving and becoming are utterly exhausted— him indeed I call a brahmin.
He for whom there is no longing in this world or even in the next, who is free from desire and detached— I indeed call him a brahmin.
Having abandoned both pleasure and displeasure, become cooled and free from substrate,
the wise one who has overcome the entire world— him indeed I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned human desires and transcended divine desires,
one who is detached from the entire world— I indeed call him a brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin whose course neither gods, gandharvas, nor humans know, and who is endowed with infinite knowledge.
He who knows his former abodes, who sees heaven and the states of woe, and who,
having reached the destruction of birth, is a sage resolute in higher knowledge—
he understands the end of suffering; him indeed I call a brahmin.
...him indeed I call a brahmin.
He who knows the passing away and the rebirth of beings in every respect, who is unattached— the Sugata, the Buddha— I call him indeed a brahmin.
He who has transcended all fetters and is indeed not distressed— unattached, a Sugata, an Awakened One— I call him a brahmin.
I call him a brahmin who is a bull, a preeminent leader, a great seer, a victor, one who cannot be led astray, a graduate, and an awakened one.
One who is a bull among men, a preeminent elephant, a great seer, and a victor;
one who is unleadable, a bath-graduate, and awakened—him I call a brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin who has overcome all things, transcended existence, crossed the flood, is free from outflows, has reached the further shore, and is utterly detached.
One who has overcome all things, transcended the past, crossed over the flood, is a leader,
has reached the further shore, and is truly detached— him I call a brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin who has transcended covetousness, who is free from idle chatter, who is devoid of evil thoughts, who is meditative, and who is free from passion.
One should not covet, nor should one engage in idle chatter; one should avoid all evils. Seated, stainless, and meditative—him I call a Brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin who is a mendicant wearing robes of dust, indifferent toward sensual pleasures, and meditating while seated at the foot of a tree.
One who wears a garment of dust, is modest, is indifferent toward sensual desires,
and sits at the foot of a tree— him I call a brahmin.
He who has no abode at all, who is the knower beyond dispute,
and who has indeed attained the deathless— him I call a brahmin.
He who has no abode, who is the knower, who is beyond dispute and free from speech, who wanders far alone— I call him indeed a brahmin.
That which goes far, moves alone, is bodiless, and dwells in the cave—by that [Brahman]... of whom am I a Brahmin? ... I call him a Brahmin.
Those for whom the noble eightfold path, which leads to peace,
has been cultivated for the sake of abandoning all suffering— they alone are the true brahmins in the worlds.

The mind is always formless, without core, and invisible; those who, having tamed it and understood it, always proceed with mindfulness— those Buddhas, whose fetters are exhausted, are indeed the brahmins in the worlds.
Formless, invisible, infinite, and difficult to behold,
having realized this subtle state, those who always practice with mindfulness— those Buddhas whose fetters are exhausted are the true brahmins in this world.
Having cut through the fetters and the leather straps, and having transcended the difficult-to-cross continuity, and having filled the moat— I call that Buddha indeed a brahmin.
Those who have severed the leather thongs and the bonds, the continuity that is so difficult to transcend,
and for whom the moat has been cast up— they are the awakened ones, the brahmins here in this world.
Having cut through the bonds and the thongs, and having severed evil desire and greed, and having uprooted craving along with its root— him indeed I call a brahmin.
Those who have cut the bonds and the thongs, as well as evil desire and greed, and have uprooted craving along with its root— they are the brahmins here in this world.
Exerting yourself, cut off the stream; O Brahmin, cast away desires!
Having realized the exhaustion of the conditioned formations, one will indeed become free from debt.
Exerting yourself, cut off the stream and cast away all desires;
knowing the exhaustion of conditioned phenomena, the Brahmin indeed goes forth, free from affliction.
Having slain his mother and father, a king, and two Vedic scholars,
and having destroyed a kingdom along with its subjects, a Brahmin goes forth free from sin.
Having killed his mother, his father, a king, two Vedic scholars,
and having killed a tiger as the fifth, a man is said to be pure.
One should not strike a brahmin, nor should a brahmin release [anger] against one; shame on the slayer of a brahmin, and shame on him who releases [his wrath].
Whosoever one may learn the Dharma from, whether he be old or young,
one should honor him and pay him homage with reverence, just as a twice-born man tends the sacred fire.
Whose dharma one may understand— whether he be old or young—
one should serve him with reverence, just as a twice-born serves the sacred fire.
One who understands the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Awakened One should honor it and pay it homage, just as a twice-born brahmin honors the sacred fire-offering.
One who would understand the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Awakened One should serve it with reverence, just as a twice-born serves the sacred fire-offering.
For when a brahmin has reached the further shore of his own duties,
he then transcends both the Piśācī and the Bakkula.
For when a brahmin has reached the further shore of his own dharmas,
then all his sensations pass away as he perceives them.
For when a brahmin has reached the further shore of his own dharmas,
then all his conceptual conditions pass away as he perceives them.
For when a brahmin has reached the further shore of his own dharmas,
then all his taints go to their setting as he perceives them.
For when a brahmin becomes one who has reached the further shore of his own duties,
then all his attachments vanish from the sight of him as he perceives.
For when a brahmin has reached the further shore of his own duties,
he then transcends birth, old age, and death.
By day the sun indeed shines; by night the moon glows.
The armored kṣatriya shines; the meditating brāhmaṇa shines.
But the Buddha always, day and night, shines with splendor.
For a brahmin, there is nothing like this: the restraint of the mind from what is dear.
For in whatever measure his mind turns away [from such things], in that same measure he attains the cessation of suffering.
But when these phenomena arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish when he understands suffering along with its cause.
But when these phenomena arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart, once he understands the Dharma along with its cause.
But when these phenomena arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart, once he has reached the destruction of the conditions.
But when these phenomena arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart, when he reaches the destruction of feelings.
But when these phenomena arise for the ardent and meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart, for he has reached the destruction of the outflows.
But when these qualities arise in a brahmin who is ardent and meditative,
he stands illuminating the entire world, just as the sun has risen in the sky.
But when these states arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin,
the Buddha— fully liberated from the fetters— remains illuminating the entire world.
But when these states arise for the ardent, meditating brahmin—
dispelling Māra’s army and remaining liberated from the fetters— he is indeed a Buddha.
The summary verse:
Impermanence, craving for sensual pleasures, heedfulness, as well as what is dear,
virtuous conduct, good speech, action, and faith— these are your ten [qualities].
The ascetic, the path, honor, malice, mindfulness, miscellaneous matters, water, flowers, and the horse— these ten are together with anger.
Likewise, *tathāgata*, *śruta*, and *ātman*; *peyāla* and *mitra* as the fifth;
*nirvāṇa*, *paśya*, *pāpa*, and *yugavarga* with *sukha*;
*citta*, *bhikṣu*, and *brāhmaṇa*—these are recorded as the thirty-three.
The sections are completed; this summary has been spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
